title: The Estate on Crestline Drive
tagline: A new conservatorship, a locked house, and a son who got there first.

client.name: Harold Nakamura
client.snapshot: Retired aerospace machinist with moderate dementia, living alone in his Pasadena home of 50 years. His daughter Keiko petitioned for conservatorship after noticing unpaid bills and strangers' cars in the driveway. His son Dennis has been 'helping with finances' for the past year — and no one can say exactly what that means.

intro: You stand on the cracked driveway of 412 Crestline Drive, certified Letters of Conservatorship in your folder, freshly issued yesterday. The court has appointed you conservator of Harold Nakamura's estate after a contested hearing where his two children barely looked at each other. Keiko says her father's accounts have been 'bleeding for a year.' Dennis says he's been keeping the household afloat and resents your appointment. Inside this house is everything you have to find, protect, value, and report to the court — and your 90-day clock for the Inventory & Appraisal started the moment Letters issued.

stages.narrative: Keiko meets you at the door with a spare key. The house is cluttered — stacks of unopened mail on the dining table, a bedroom dresser with jewelry boxes, and a den full of filing cabinets. Dennis calls your cell while you're standing in the entryway: 'I have my own key. I'll come by this week and pull together Dad's papers for you. I know where everything is.'
stages.prompt: It's your first day marshaling the estate. How do you take control of Harold's assets and records?

options.text: Rekey the house, search room by room with a witness present, photograph valuables for an asset list, and redirect Harold's mail to your office.
options.outcome: By the end of the week you control the house, the mail, and a documented snapshot of the estate. The redirected mail starts surfacing bank statements, a brokerage notice, and a small key in a coin envelope.
options.explanation: Marshaling means locating and taking control of assets immediately. The recommended practice is a physical search with a witness present for your own liability protection, photographic documentation of personal property before values are assigned, and a change of address so financial mail — the single best asset-location tool — flows to you. Securing the residence (rekeying) prevents anyone with a key, including family, from removing property before it is inventoried.

options.text: Search the house yourself today and start a detailed asset list, planning to handle the locks and the mail redirect once you've seen what's there.
options.outcome: You build a solid asset list, but a week passes before the locks are changed, and Dennis visits the house twice in the meantime. You can't prove anything is missing — but you also can't prove nothing is.
options.explanation: Searching promptly is right, but this is inferior on two specific points: searching alone leaves you without a witness if anyone later claims property disappeared on your watch, and delaying the rekeying and mail redirect leaves the estate's two most vulnerable channels — the house and the mailbox — open to interference. Control first, then catalog.

options.text: Accept Dennis's offer to gather all of Harold's papers himself — he knows where everything is, and cooperating keeps the family case running smoothly.
options.outcome: Dennis delivers a tidy folder of papers two weeks later. It contains no brokerage statements, and the dresser jewelry boxes are noticeably lighter than Keiko remembers.
options.explanation: The duty to marshal assets is yours and cannot be delegated to an interested family member — especially one whose past handling of the finances is exactly what triggered the conservatorship. Allowing a potentially adverse party unsupervised control of records and access to property fails the duty to locate and control assets and compromises the integrity of your inventory.

stages.narrative: The redirected mail pays off fast. A quarterly statement arrives from a brokerage Keiko never knew existed: $480,000 in mutual funds and a money market, all in Harold's name alone. The problem — your bond was set at the hearing based on the petition's estimate of a $150,000 estate.
stages.prompt: The estate is more than three times the size the court bonded you for. What do you do?

options.text: Notify your attorney and the court promptly and seek a larger bond or a blocked account.
options.outcome: The court orders the bulk of the brokerage funds into a blocked account and a modest bond increase for the rest. The estate is fully protected, and the judge notes your prompt disclosure favorably.
options.explanation: The bond protects the conservatee: it must cover the value of personal property plus estimated annual income and benefits, plus an additional percentage for recovery costs. When you discover the estate materially exceeds the bonded amount, the conservatee is unprotected for the difference — you must act now, not later. A blocked account, which permits withdrawals only on court order, is the recognized alternative that lets the court reduce or waive bond while keeping assets safe.

options.text: Have your attorney address the bond increase when you file the Inventory & Appraisal, which will officially set the estate's value anyway.
options.outcome: The bond is eventually corrected, but for nearly two months a $480,000 account sat exposed with only $150,000 of surety protection — a gap the court's examiner flags in a written notice.
options.explanation: Tying the bond to the I&A filing is administratively tidy and many fiduciaries think this way, but it is inferior because the conservatee bears unbonded risk during the entire delay. The duty to protect the estate means correcting a known bond deficiency promptly upon discovery — the I&A deadline is a separate obligation, not the trigger for fixing the bond.

options.text: Leave the brokerage account exactly as-is until your first accounting — the funds sit at an established firm and they aren't going anywhere soon.
options.outcome: A year later the court examiner discovers the discrepancy in your first accounting and issues a notice demanding an explanation for twelve months of inadequate bonding.
options.explanation: Waiting until the first accounting ignores the entire purpose of the bond, which exists so the surety can make the estate whole if anything goes wrong in the interim. A fiduciary who knows the estate is under-bonded and does nothing has failed the duty of care, and courts treat unexplained delays in protecting assets as a supervision red flag.

stages.narrative: Day 60. The probate referee has appraised the house and most of the personal property, but Harold's den held a surprise: a serious rare-coin collection, and the referee wants a specialist's input before assigning a value. The specialist is booked out six weeks. Your Inventory & Appraisal is due at day 90.
stages.prompt: The coin appraisal won't be done before the I&A deadline. How do you handle the filing?

options.text: File a partial I&A by day 90 for the appraised items, then a final partial for the coins.
options.outcome: You file on time with everything but the coins, noting the pending specialist appraisal. The final partial follows five weeks later, and together the inventories account for all property.
options.explanation: The Inventory & Appraisal must be filed within 90 days of appointment, and the recognized procedure when items are still being appraised is exactly this: file partial inventories followed by a final partial, with all partials together totaling all of the estate's property. This meets the statutory deadline without compromising the accuracy of the appraisal — both of which are your responsibility to the court.

options.text: Have your attorney request a court extension of the I&A deadline before day 90, explaining the specialist delay.
options.outcome: The court grants a short extension, but the file now shows the estate's required snapshot arriving late — and your fee request is pushed back too, since fees can't be requested until the I&A is on file.
options.explanation: Seeking an extension before the deadline is a legitimate, defensible move — far better than blowing the date. But it's inferior to the partial-inventory procedure, which exists precisely for this situation and gets the bulk of the estate on record on time. Note the practical cost: a conservator cannot request fees until 90 days after appointment AND the I&A is filed, so delay costs you and delays the court's full picture of the estate.

options.text: File a complete I&A on time using your own good-faith estimate of the coin collection's value, drawn from online price guides and recent listings.
options.outcome: The filing is rejected for correction: the coins were appraised by you rather than the referee, and your guidebook number turns out to be $30,000 under the specialist's eventual figure.
options.explanation: The probate referee — not the conservator — appraises estate assets; the conservator values only cash-type items. Substituting your own estimate for unique collectibles bypasses the referee system, understates or overstates the estate the bond and accountings are built on, and is exactly why specialized appraisers exist for coins, art, jewelry, and antiques.

stages.narrative: The coin collection and the dresser jewelry are still sitting in an empty house that everyone in the family knows is unoccupied. Dennis calls again, friendlier this time: 'Dad always said I'd get his Rolex. It's just sitting there. Let me hold onto it — sentimental value, you understand.'
stages.prompt: How do you handle the valuable personal property — and Dennis's request?

options.text: Photograph the valuables with a witness, move them to insured storage titled to the estate, and tell Dennis the watch stays — bequests pass through the will.
options.outcome: The coins and jewelry are documented, insured, and locked away. Dennis grumbles but can't argue with 'everything is preserved exactly as your father left it, for whoever he left it to.'
options.explanation: Safekeeping duties require documenting personal property with photos and descriptions before values are assigned, keeping it in a separate secure location, and insuring it. Distributing property now — even an item the conservatee allegedly promised — would prejudge the estate plan: specific bequests are honored at death through the will, not handed out by the conservator. Holding the line preserves both the asset and Harold's testamentary intent.

options.text: Rekey the house again, add an alarm, confirm the homeowner's policy covers contents, and leave the valuables where they are, since moving them carries its own risks.
options.outcome: Nothing goes missing, but your insurance broker warns that the unoccupied-dwelling clause may limit contents coverage, and the court investigator asks why high-value portables are sitting in a vacant house.
options.explanation: Securing and insuring property in place is a defensible safekeeping approach for furniture and bulky items. It's inferior here because small, high-value, easily portable items — coins, jewelry, a luxury watch — are precisely what safe deposit boxes are for, and vacant-house insurance often restricts contents coverage. The standard is what a prudent fiduciary would do with someone else's irreplaceable property, and that means the bank vault.

options.text: Let Dennis take the Rolex for now but have him sign a written receipt acknowledging that the watch remains property of the conservatorship estate.
options.outcome: Six months later Dennis claims the watch was a completed gift from his father years ago. Your receipt helps, but the estate now needs a court proceeding to recover one watch.
options.explanation: A receipt doesn't cure the underlying error: releasing estate property to an interested family member before the court has authorized any distribution. You've converted a secured asset into a disputed claim, handed leverage to the person the family conflict centers on, and created recovery costs the estate shouldn't bear. Possession of estate property is yours to maintain, not to lend.

stages.narrative: The bank records arrive, and the picture darkens. A checking account titled jointly with Dennis shows $40,000 in withdrawals over the past six months — ATM cash, transfers to Dennis's own account, a payment to a car dealership. And the small key from the coin envelope matches a safe deposit box at the same bank that no one mentioned in the petition.
stages.prompt: You're looking at a possible $40,000 hole in the estate and an unexplored safe deposit box. What's your move?

options.text: Open the box with a bank officer, check whether the joint account was true ownership or convenience, report the suspected abuse, and ask counsel about recovery.
options.outcome: The box holds savings bonds and Harold's original will. The account history shows Dennis was added 'for convenience' two years ago when Harold's memory failed. The court orders Dennis to account for every withdrawal.
options.explanation: A fiduciary must determine whether joint accounts are truly jointly owned or were set up for convenience — the answer controls whether those funds belong to the estate. The withdrawals match classic exploitation indicators (cash, transfers, purchases benefiting the joint holder), and as a mandatory reporter you must report suspected financial abuse; there is no conflict of interest in filing an APS report. Recovery belongs in court, with bank protocols and witnesses protecting the integrity of everything you touch.

options.text: Confront Dennis with the records and negotiate a written repayment plan, keeping the matter inside the family to preserve relationships Harold would want intact.
options.outcome: Dennis signs a repayment agreement and makes two payments before stopping. You've lost months, the trail has cooled, and you never made the abuse report the law expected of you.
options.explanation: Pursuing recovery is right, and informal resolution feels humane — but it's inferior because it substitutes your private judgment for the court's oversight on a matter squarely within the court's supervision, and it skips your mandatory reporting obligation for suspected financial abuse. A private deal with the suspected abuser also has no teeth: when it collapses, the estate has lost time, evidence freshness, and leverage.

options.text: Treat the joint account as Dennis's own property — his name is on the title, so the withdrawals he made were legally his to make without question.
options.outcome: Keiko's attorney later establishes the account was funded entirely with Harold's pension deposits, and the court asks why the conservator surrendered $40,000 without a single question.
options.explanation: Title alone doesn't answer the ownership question. Joint accounts are frequently established for convenience — to help an aging parent pay bills — without any intent to gift the funds. The fiduciary's duty is to investigate the source of funds and the circumstances of the account's creation before conceding estate assets, especially where the pattern of withdrawals screams exploitation.

stages.narrative: With the drama contained, it's time to build the financial machinery this estate will run on for years: bills to pay, pension and Social Security flowing in, the blocked account, and a court accounting due at the one-year mark that will scrutinize every dollar in and out.
stages.prompt: How do you set up the estate's banking and records?

options.text: Open a conservatorship account titled to you as Harold's conservator, route all income through it, keep it separate from other funds, and retain receipts.
options.outcome: A year later, your first accounting assembles cleanly — every receipt and disbursement traceable, schedules balanced to the penny. The examiner has no questions.
options.explanation: All conservatee money must flow through a properly titled conservatorship account in the conservator's name, never commingled with personal funds or other clients' funds. Court accountings require opening values, every receipt, every disbursement, gains and losses, and closing values organized by schedule — a record-keeping standard you can only meet if the account structure and document retention are built correctly from day one. The fiduciary operates as an open book with a complete paper trail.

options.text: Open the conservatorship account, but track activity through your accounting software and bank statements rather than keeping every paper invoice and receipt.
options.outcome: The accounting balances, but when the examiner asks for backup on three caregiver payments and a $2,800 home repair, you have bank entries and memory rather than invoices — and a follow-up letter to answer.
options.explanation: The account structure is right, which is the biggest decision. But statements alone show that money moved, not why — and the reasonableness of each disbursement is exactly what the court reviews. Accurate records means source documentation: invoices showing what was bought, from whom, and for whose benefit. Thin backup turns routine accountings into correspondence with the examiner.

options.text: Keep paying bills from Harold's existing account using the signature stamp Dennis had made — it's already linked to all the autopays.
options.outcome: The bank freezes the account when it learns Harold is conserved, three autopays bounce, and the court examiner asks why estate funds were moving under a signature device created during the period of suspected abuse.
options.explanation: Your authority comes from Letters of Conservatorship, and assets must be retitled to reflect the fiduciary relationship — banks require certified Letters to recognize you. Operating someone's old account through a signature stamp is not fiduciary control; it perpetuates the broken arrangement that necessitated the conservatorship and produces records no court can rely on.

epilogues.triumph: At the first accounting hearing, the judge takes a rare moment on the record: the I&A was timely, the bond corrected promptly, the exploitation caught and $34,000 recovered from Dennis. Keiko thanks you in the hallway, and within a month the court appoints you on two new matters on the examiner's quiet recommendation.
epilogues.solid: The accounting is approved with a couple of examiner questions you're able to answer. Harold's estate is secure and his care funded, though you know a few early gaps — the bonding delay, the missing receipts — made the year harder than it needed to be. A competent first conservatorship, with lessons attached.
epilogues.shaky: The court approves the accounting but with a written admonishment: late protective steps, thin documentation, and an exploitation issue that should have reached the court sooner. The judge orders more frequent status reports, and you can feel the investigator reading your filings more carefully now.
epilogues.disaster: The hearing is brutal. Unrecovered funds, commingled accounts, a blown deadline — the judge surcharges you for the estate's losses, orders your bond carrier notified, and sets a hearing on your removal. Keiko's new attorney mentions the Professional Fiduciaries Bureau complaint form on the way out.

title: The House on Magnolia Court
tagline: Selling a conservatee's home means selling the one place the law tells you to protect.

client.name: Rosa Delgado
client.snapshot: A widowed seamstress who raised four children in her Whittier bungalow and never spent a night anywhere else until a major stroke eight months ago. She now lives in a residential care facility, her speech limited but her eyes going straight to the photo of the house on her nightstand. Her savings will cover about ten more months of care.

intro: You've been Rosa Delgado's conservator of the estate for eight months, and the spreadsheet on your screen says what nobody in her family wants to hear: at $7,400 a month for her care facility, her liquid assets run out by spring. The bungalow on Magnolia Court — appraised by the probate referee at $610,000 in your Inventory & Appraisal — is the estate's only major asset. Her niece Carmen calls it 'Tía Rosa's whole life' and swears she'll fight any sale. Her nephew Mateo says his contractor friend will pay cash this week, no realtors, no fuss. Between them stands you, the law's special protection for a conservatee's personal residence, and a court that will scrutinize every step.

stages.narrative: Rosa's care team is unanimous: she needs 24-hour assistance and cannot safely return home, even with in-home care, given her fall risk and swallowing issues. Carmen insists Rosa would rather die at home. Mateo wants the house sold yesterday. The money runs out in ten months either way.
stages.prompt: The estate needs the home's value, but it's Rosa's personal residence. How do you approach the decision to sell?

options.text: Build the record first: get medical proof she can't return, weigh alternatives like renting, then notice and petition to sell.
options.outcome: Your petition lays out the care evidence, the rental analysis showing net income would cover barely a third of her care cost, and Rosa's own statement, gathered with her speech therapist's help, that she 'wants the garden to go to a family.' The court grants authority to sell.
options.explanation: The law gives special protection to the conservatee's personal residence — the home she believed was permanent. A sale requires demonstrating why it serves her needs, not anyone's convenience, after considering less drastic alternatives, with prior notice to the court and those close to her. Building the medical and financial record first, and applying substituted judgment by capturing Rosa's actual wishes, is exactly what the court expects before this most sensitive of asset decisions.

options.text: Petition the court for authority to sell now — the financial math is undeniable, and the confirmation process will give everyone a chance to object.
options.outcome: The court continues your hearing twice, asking for medical evidence that Rosa cannot return home and an analysis of alternatives — the very record you skipped. You get there, but three months later, with Carmen's objection now organized and angry.
options.explanation: Going to court for authority is the right instinct, and the financial need is real — that's what makes this attractive. But it's inferior because the personal-residence preference puts the burden on you to show, before seeking the sale, that return is infeasible and that alternatives were considered. A petition resting on money alone invites continuances, objections, and the appearance that the sale is for administrative convenience rather than Rosa's needs.

options.text: Take Mateo's contractor friend up on the cash offer this week — a fast private sale avoids months of carrying costs on a vacant, deteriorating house.
options.outcome: Your attorney stops you before papers are signed: the sale needs court confirmation, the buyer's 'cash offer' is $85,000 under the referee's appraisal, and Mateo's involvement reeks of a deal benefiting everyone but Rosa.
options.explanation: A conservator cannot simply sell a conservatee's real property — let alone her protected personal residence — by private handshake. Court confirmation requirements exist precisely to prevent insider sales at below-market prices, and a deal sourced by a family member with his own agenda fails the test that every decision serve the conservatee's best interest. The savings on carrying costs would be dwarfed by the value sacrificed.

stages.narrative: Authority granted, you need the house on the market. Mateo announces he has a real estate license and offers to list it himself 'at a family discount.' Meanwhile your office files hold a card from the agent you've used on your last several cases — reliable, but she mostly does standard resales.
stages.prompt: How do you choose who sells the house?

options.text: Interview several agents, verify licensing and insurance, favor probate-confirmation experience, and list on the MLS.
options.outcome: You sign with an agent who's closed dozens of court-confirmed sales. She prices to the referee's appraisal, papers the file for confirmation from day one, and the listing draws six showings the first weekend.
options.explanation: Selecting professionals for an estate is itself a fiduciary act: verify licensing and insurance, and look specifically for experience with fiduciary sales, because court confirmation, the 90% appraisal rule, and publication requirements trip up agents who've never seen them. Competitive selection and full MLS exposure maximize the price for Rosa — the only client whose interest counts here.

options.text: Hire the agent you've worked with on past cases — you know her work, she knows your standards, and speed matters with the estate's runway shrinking.
options.outcome: The listing goes live quickly, but the agent stumbles on the confirmation mechanics — she's never handled an overbid hearing — and her unfamiliarity later costs you a delay you couldn't afford.
options.explanation: Using a known, competent professional isn't misconduct, and continuity has real value — that's what makes this defensible. It's inferior because you skipped the comparison that demonstrates the choice served Rosa rather than your own convenience, and because fiduciary sales reward specialized experience: an agent fluent in court confirmation protects the timeline and price in ways general resale experience doesn't. Document why your professional choices serve the client.

options.text: Let Mateo list the house himself — he's a licensed, motivated family member, and the discounted commission he's offering saves the estate real money.
options.outcome: Carmen's attorney fires off an objection within days: the conservator has hired an interested family member — one pushing his friend's lowball offer weeks ago — to control the sale of the asset he stands to inherit from.
options.explanation: Hiring family members to provide estate services is prohibited when reasonable alternatives exist, and where it's even considered, it demands full disclosure to the court and proof the terms beat independent providers. Mateo is an heir with a demonstrated agenda in this very transaction — an unmanageable conflict of interest no commission discount can cure. The savings would cost the sale its integrity.

stages.narrative: Three weeks on market produce a strong offer: $585,000. Your agent is ready to draft the confirmation petition. Then your attorney's paralegal flags the file: the probate referee's $610,000 appraisal was completed nine months ago, back at the I&A.
stages.prompt: The offer is on the table and the appraisal is nine months old. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the probate referee to reappraise first, since the value is over six months old, then confirm the offer clears 90%.
options.outcome: The referee reappraises at $595,000, reflecting a cooling market. Your $585,000 offer comfortably clears 90% of current value, and your confirmation petition sails through review with no defects.
options.explanation: Two distinct rules govern here: the sale price must be at least 90% of the referee's appraised value, AND the appraisal must be current — a reappraisal is required if the property was appraised more than six months before the sale. A stale appraisal is one of the classic petition defects that gets confirmations rejected. Reappraising first ensures the 90% test is run against a number the court will actually accept.

options.text: Proceed on the original appraisal — $585,000 is 96% of $610,000, well above the 90% floor, so the offer clearly qualifies.
options.outcome: The court's probate examiner bounces the petition: the appraisal is over six months old and must be refreshed before confirmation. You lose five weeks re-running what you could have done up front, while the buyer gets restless.
options.explanation: The math is exactly right, which is why this feels safe — and it shows you know the 90% rule. But it's inferior because the 90% test and the six-month recency requirement are independent: a price can pass the percentage handily and still fail confirmation because the appraisal itself is stale. Markets move; the court demands the comparison be made against current value, not last year's.

options.text: Hire an independent fee appraiser to produce an updated value quickly — far faster than waiting in the probate referee's reappraisal queue.
options.outcome: The private appraisal arrives quickly and reads beautifully, but the examiner's notes are blunt: confirmation requires the probate referee's appraisal, and the estate just paid for a report the court won't use.
options.explanation: In court-supervised sales, the probate referee is the court's appointed appraiser, and the 90% rule runs against the referee's figure. A private appraisal may inform your pricing strategy, but it cannot substitute for the referee's reappraisal in the confirmation process. Paying for the wrong appraisal wastes estate funds and the time it was meant to save.

stages.narrative: Your attorney is assembling the confirmation petition and runs the checklist with you. The listing has been everywhere — MLS, Zillow, the agent's social media, an open house that drew forty people. 'One more thing,' she says. 'Notice of sale. Where did we publish?'
stages.prompt: How do you satisfy the notice requirements for the sale?

options.text: Publish notice of sale in a newspaper of general circulation, keep the proof for the petition, and confirm it ran within the year.
options.outcome: The notice runs, the proof of publication goes into the petition exhibits, and at the hearing the judge ticks through the checklist without pausing. The sale is cleared for confirmation.
options.explanation: Court-supervised real property sales require published notice in a newspaper — MLS and online marketing, however extensive, do not satisfy the statutory publication requirement. The publication must occur within one year prior to the sale, and the proof of publication must be filed; forgetting publication is one of the most common reasons courts reject confirmation petitions. Compliance here is mechanical, cheap, and absolutely mandatory.

options.text: Document the marketing campaign — MLS, portals, open houses, forty attendees — and present it as notice reaching far more buyers than any newspaper could.
options.outcome: Your marketing exhibit is genuinely impressive, and the judge says so — right before continuing the hearing because there is no proof of newspaper publication in the file. Three more weeks of carrying costs while the notice runs.
options.explanation: You're factually right that modern marketing out-reaches a legal notice in a newspaper nobody reads — which is exactly why this answer tempts good fiduciaries. But it's inferior because publication is a statutory requirement, not a marketing standard: the court has no discretion to accept MLS exposure as a substitute. The exam loves this distinction — the legally required step beats the practically superior one when the statute speaks.

options.text: Skip the newspaper publication entirely — every family member already has actual notice, the hearing itself is public, and the buyer came from full exposure.
options.outcome: The petition is rejected for the missing proof of publication. Actual notice to the family turns out to be an answer to a question nobody asked.
options.explanation: Publication serves a different function than family notice: it alerts the public — including potential overbidders — that estate property is being sold, supporting the competitive process that protects the conservatee's price. Family awareness, however complete, cannot substitute for the public notice the statute requires. Missing proof of publication is a per se defect, not a harmless one.

stages.narrative: The buyer's final terms: $585,000, all cash, as-is, quick close. During your last walkthrough before the hearing, you notice the ceiling stain in the back bedroom has spread — the roofer you called confirms active leaking and quotes $18,000. The buyer hasn't asked about the roof.
stages.prompt: It's an as-is, all-cash probate sale and you know about the roof. What are your obligations?

options.text: Disclose the known roof defect in writing despite as-is terms, verify proof of funds since 'all cash' drops the financing contingency, and document removals.
options.outcome: The buyer grumbles, negotiates a modest credit, and proceeds — with the defect disclosed, funds verified, and contingencies removed in writing, the confirmation hearing has nothing to snag on.
options.explanation: In probate sales, 'as is' has a specific legal meaning — the buyer investigates and purchases as-is, and the fiduciary is exempt from most standard seller disclosures — BUT the fiduciary must still disclose known defects. You know about the roof, so you must disclose it. 'All cash' likewise has a precise meaning: the financing contingency is removed, which makes verifying proof of funds essential. Contingencies not removed in writing are among the classic confirmation errors.

options.text: Hold the sale, repair the roof for $18,000, and relist — a sound house commands a better price and eliminates the disclosure issue entirely.
options.outcome: The buyer walks rather than wait. The repair takes six weeks, the relaunch finds a softer market, and the eventual price improvement roughly equals the repair cost — minus three more months of care expenses the estate paid while you waited.
options.explanation: Repairing before sale is a legitimate strategy a reasonable fiduciary might choose, and it shows good instincts about value — that's its appeal. It's inferior here because it solves a problem disclosure already solves at zero cost and zero delay: the as-is framework exists so estates can sell without undertaking repairs, and Rosa's shrinking runway makes time itself an asset. The cheaper, faster path that fully satisfies your legal duty is to disclose and let the buyer price it.

options.text: Say nothing about the roof — it's an as-is sale, the buyer holds full inspection rights, and a fiduciary need not investigate or volunteer the property's flaws.
options.outcome: The buyer's post-closing contractor finds the leak in twenty minutes and the demand letter arrives in a week, alleging concealment of a known defect by a court-appointed fiduciary.
options.explanation: This answer is built on a half-truth, which makes it dangerous: a fiduciary genuinely is NOT obligated to inspect beyond their own knowledge and is exempt from most standard disclosures. But the exemption has a hard edge — known defects must be disclosed. You called the roofer; you know. As-is shifts the risk of unknown problems to the buyer, never the seller's silence about known ones.

stages.narrative: Confirmation day. The courtroom holds your buyer's agent, Carmen with crossed arms — and a stranger in a windbreaker who rises when the judge calls for overbids. He offers $620,000 and pulls out a personal check for his ten percent deposit. The judge looks to counsel. The buyer's agent objects. Carmen looks delighted by the chaos.
stages.prompt: An overbidder has appeared with a higher price and a personal check. How do you respond?

options.text: Support the overbid on its terms: it must hit the statutory minimum and the deposit must be a cashier's check. Otherwise, ask the court to confirm the buyer.
options.outcome: The judge gives the overbidder until the matter recalls that afternoon; he returns with a cashier's check, and the court confirms the sale at $620,000 — $35,000 more for Rosa's care. Escrow opens on the confirmation order.
options.explanation: The overbid process exists for one reason: to squeeze maximum value out of the estate's property for the conservatee. Your role is to facilitate it correctly, not to defend the original deal. The rules are specific — an overbidder must present a cashier's check, not a personal check, for the required deposit on the overbid amount. Knowing the mechanics lets you protect both the price and the procedure, and the sale closes through escrow only after the court's confirmation.

options.text: Ask the court for a short continuance to remarket at the higher number — if one stranger will pay $620,000, an organized overbid round might find more.
options.outcome: The judge declines; the statutory overbid process at today's hearing IS the competitive mechanism. You've signaled willingness to delay a closing the estate urgently needs in pursuit of speculative upside.
options.explanation: Chasing maximum value is the right instinct, and there are cases where remarketing makes sense — that's the lure. But it's inferior because the confirmation hearing's open overbidding already supplies court-supervised price competition, and a continuance risks losing both bidders while Rosa's care costs run. The fiduciary's judgment weighs a bird in hand secured by court order against an unsecured maybe — with the estate's liquidity nearly gone, the qualified overbid wins.

options.text: Oppose the overbid outright — the original buyer negotiated in good faith for months, took the roof disclosure, and basic fairness says the deal should be theirs.
options.outcome: The judge cuts you off mid-sentence: 'Counsel, whose interest does the conservator represent?' The overbid is accepted over your objection, and your protest is now part of the record.
options.explanation: Loyalty in this transaction runs to exactly one person: Rosa. The original buyer's effort and patience are commercial risks every probate buyer knowingly accepts — overbidding at confirmation is a published feature of the process. A conservator arguing against $35,000 of additional value for the conservatee, out of fairness to a stranger, has the duty of loyalty exactly backwards.

epilogues.triumph: Escrow closes at $620,000, netting Rosa years of secure care. At the next status hearing the judge calls the sale 'a model of how these are done,' and Carmen — of all people — sends a note: the buyer's family planted tomatoes where Rosa's used to be, and she's taken Rosa by to see them. Your phone starts ringing with referrals from the probate bar.
epilogues.solid: The house sells and Rosa's care is funded — the outcome that mattered. The file shows a few detours: a continued hearing here, a stale appraisal there. The judge approves everything with the mild observation that 'the second conservatorship sale is always smoother than the first.' You intend to prove it.
epilogues.shaky: The sale closes, but late and lean, after rejected petitions and examiner notices ate months of Rosa's runway. The court approves the transaction while ordering supplemental reporting on the estate's diminished liquidity, and Carmen's attorney now copies the investigator on everything. You've kept the case — barely.
epilogues.disaster: Between the botched marketing, the defective petitions, and the questions surrounding your conduct at confirmation, the court vacates the sale, surcharges you for the estate's losses and wasted costs, and grants Carmen's petition for your removal. The successor conservator's first call is to the Professional Fiduciaries Bureau. The second is to your bond carrier.

title: The Settlement
tagline: A million dollars can ruin a life on SSI — unless the trustee knows exactly what they're doing.

client.name: Damian Carter
client.snapshot: A former warehouse lead who survived a delivery-truck collision with a traumatic brain injury that left him with impaired memory, seizures, and limited mobility. He lives with his mother Tanya, receives SSI and Medi-Cal, and is about to receive a $1.1 million net personal-injury settlement. He is sharp enough to know what he wants and disabled enough to need every benefit he has.

intro: You're in a conference room with Damian Carter, his mother Tanya, and his personal-injury attorney, who slides the settlement breakdown across the table: $1.1 million net to Damian. Everyone is smiling except you, because you can see the cliff nobody else sees — Damian's SSI has a $2,000 asset limit, his Medi-Cal pays for the seizure medication that costs $3,100 a month, and the settlement check will destroy both the moment it touches his name. The attorney wants to know how you'd structure things as trustee. Damian's grandmother Pearl, sitting quietly in the corner, mentions she's also updating her will to 'leave my grandson something real.' Every dollar in this room needs a different home.

stages.narrative: The settlement attorney asks the threshold question: where does Damian's money go? Pearl repeats that her own will currently leaves Damian $200,000 outright. Two pools of money, two different sets of rules — and one beneficiary whose benefits hang on getting it right.
stages.prompt: How should the settlement — and Pearl's planned bequest — be structured?

options.text: Put the settlement in a court-established first-party SNT, and redirect Pearl's bequest into a third-party SNT with no Medicaid payback.
options.outcome: The settlement funds a first-party SNT with you as trustee; Pearl's estate plan is rewritten so her $200,000 will flow to a separate third-party SNT. Damian's SSI and Medi-Cal continue without interruption.
options.explanation: The source of funds dictates the trust. The settlement is Damian's own money, so preserving his benefits requires a first-party (d)(4)(A) SNT — beneficiary under 65, disabled, established with court involvement — which must be for his sole benefit and must repay Medi-Cal at his death. Pearl's money is third-party money: routed to a third-party SNT it supplements his needs with NO Medicaid payback and far less government oversight. Mixing the two pools would needlessly subject Pearl's gift to payback.

options.text: Join a nonprofit-managed pooled special needs trust for the settlement — professional administration, established SSA acceptance, and lower setup costs.
options.outcome: The pooled trust accepts the funds and benefits are preserved, but its standardized distribution policies chafe against Damian's specific needs, and the master trust terms leave less room for the tailored management $1.1 million deserves.
options.explanation: A first-party pooled (d)(4)(C) trust is a fully legitimate vehicle — nonprofit-established, separate accounts, benefits-safe — and often the right answer for modest sums or when no individual trustee is available. It's inferior here because Damian has both a seven-figure corpus that justifies individualized trust administration and a professional trustee standing ready: you. Pooled trusts trade flexibility for convenience; with this much money and a 50-year horizon, flexibility is worth more.

options.text: Open an ABLE account and deposit the entire settlement into it — the growth is tax-free and, you assume, it won't affect his SSI or Medi-Cal benefits.
options.outcome: The ABLE program rejects the deposit: contributions are capped at $20,000 this year, and account balances above $100,000 start counting against SSI anyway. Meanwhile the settlement sits in limbo, threatening his eligibility.
options.explanation: ABLE accounts are a powerful supplement — Damian qualifies, since his disability onset falls under the age limit — but they cannot absorb a $1.1 million settlement: annual contributions are limited ($20,000 in 2026) and SSI excludes only the first $100,000 of ABLE balance. ABLE complements an SNT; it cannot replace one for a sum of this size.

stages.narrative: The trust is funded and word travels fast. Tanya calls: 'Damian wants some independence — can the trust just give him $800 a month for spending money? He's 26, not a child.' She's not wrong about the dignity point, and you can hear Damian in the background agreeing.
stages.prompt: How do you get money working for Damian's daily life without breaking his benefits?

options.text: Decline cash, pay his vendors and bills directly, and give him an administrator-managed restricted prepaid card for spending.
options.outcome: The trust autopays his phone, transit card, gym, and streaming services, and Damian carries a restricted card he controls for day-to-day choices. His SSI check doesn't drop a dollar, and he tells Tanya it feels like his own money — because functionally it is.
options.explanation: The distribution hierarchy runs from safest to most dangerous: trustee purchases items directly, trustee pays vendors directly (the workhorse method — use autopay), and administrator-managed restricted cards that can't access cash or prohibited categories. Cash to the beneficiary is unearned income reducing SSI dollar-for-dollar after the first $20. This answer honors person-centered practice — maximizing Damian's real autonomy — through mechanisms that keep every dollar non-countable.

options.text: Decline the cash and pay all of Damian's expenses directly to vendors yourself — the safest possible administration, with every disbursement documented.
options.outcome: Benefits stay perfectly intact, but Damian has to route every minor want through your office. By month three he's stopped asking for small things, and Tanya tells you he feels like 'a kid on an allowance he can't even hold.'
options.explanation: Direct vendor payment is the gold-standard safe method, and a trustee who does only this is legally beyond reproach — that's the appeal. It's inferior because it ignores the person-centered half of the job: restricted prepaid cards exist precisely to give beneficiaries dignity and daily choice at near-zero benefits risk, and a 26-year-old's self-determination is part of his best interest. Maximum protection that suffocates the person it protects isn't the best answer — it's just the safest-feeling one.

options.text: Add Damian as an authorized user with a debit card on the trust's own checking account — full independence for him, and you can monitor every transaction online.
options.outcome: At redetermination, SSA treats the entire trust checking account as Damian's available resource — he had unrestricted access to it. Eligibility collapses, and unwinding the determination takes a year of appeals.
options.explanation: Direct beneficiary access to trust funds is the cardinal structural sin of SNT administration: a debit card on the trust account makes the account itself a countable resource, because resources include anything the beneficiary has the legal ability to access and spend. Monitoring transactions after the fact is irrelevant — it's the unrestricted access, not the spending, that destroys eligibility. This single convenience can vaporize the entire plan.

stages.narrative: Six months in, Damian raises something bigger: he wants out of his mother's house and into an accessible one-bedroom near his day program — $1,900 a month. His only income is SSI. The apartment would transform his independence, his mood, and frankly his relationship with Tanya, which is fraying under one roof.
stages.prompt: Rent is shelter, and shelter is ISM. Can the trust pay for the apartment?

options.text: Run the analysis, then pay the landlord directly and accept the capped SSI hit — about $351 a month under the PMV rule — documenting the trade-off.
options.outcome: Damian moves in. His SSI drops by the PMV cap but keeps flowing — preserving his Medi-Cal link — and the trust absorbs the rent. His seizure log improves, his day-program attendance hits 100%, and Tanya admits the move saved their relationship.
options.explanation: Trust-paid shelter is in-kind support and maintenance (ISM) — and since September 2024, ISM counts only shelter, not food. But the penalty is capped: the presumed maximum value reduction is one-third of the federal benefit rate plus $20 (about $351/month in 2026), not a dollar-for-dollar loss. Trading a capped ~$351 reduction for housing that transforms the beneficiary's life is classic good SNT administration — eyes open, landlord paid directly, trade-off documented. SSI keeps flowing, so categorical Medi-Cal stays intact.

options.text: Decline to pay shelter from the trust to keep his SSI fully intact, and help him pursue subsidized housing waitlists instead.
options.outcome: His SSI stays whole, but the accessible-unit waitlists run two to four years. Damian stays in a living situation that's visibly wearing on him, protected in full from a benefits reduction that was capped at $351 anyway.
options.explanation: This is the conservative trustee's reflex, and it's genuinely defensible — preserving benefits is a core SNT purpose, and subsidized housing is worth pursuing in parallel. It's inferior because it treats any SSI reduction as unacceptable when the ISM rules deliberately cap the cost at the PMV. The trust exists to improve Damian's life, not to maximize a government check; refusing a life-changing expenditure to avoid a capped, affordable penalty elevates the tool above its purpose.

options.text: Give Damian the $1,900 in cash each month so he can pay the rent himself — it's the same money, and it keeps the trust out of the landlord relationship entirely.
options.outcome: The monthly $1,900 is unearned income that wipes out his entire SSI check — and when SSI hits zero, his categorical Medi-Cal link goes with it. The 'simpler' route costs him everything the PMV cap would have protected.
options.explanation: The delivery mechanism is the whole game: cash to the beneficiary is unearned income reducing SSI dollar-for-dollar after $20 — $1,900 cash eliminates his benefit entirely and severs SSI-linked Medi-Cal. The identical rent paid directly to the landlord is ISM, capped at ~$351. Same dollars, same apartment, catastrophically different outcomes. This distinction is the single most tested concept in SNT administration.

stages.narrative: At the annual review, your benefits consultant looks at the rent line and slides a brochure across the table: CalABLE. 'You know there's a way to pay that rent with no ISM reduction at all, right?' Damian's disability began at 24, well within eligibility.
stages.prompt: Can an ABLE account improve on the trust-pays-landlord arrangement?

options.text: Open a CalABLE account in Damian's name, fund it from the SNT up to the annual limit, and pay rent from it — ABLE-paid shelter carries no ISM penalty.
options.outcome: Rent now flows through CalABLE and the ~$351 monthly reduction disappears — over $4,200 a year back in Damian's pocket. He manages the ABLE account himself with light oversight, gaining both money and a real measure of financial adulthood.
options.explanation: This is the signature SNT-ABLE combination: an SNT may fund a beneficiary's ABLE account (contribution limit $20,000 in 2026), and qualified disability expenses paid from ABLE — including food and shelter — trigger NO ISM penalty. Growth is tax-free, up to $100,000 of ABLE balance is excluded from SSI resources, and CalABLE adds Medicaid payback protection on the account at death. Eligibility extends to disability onset before age 46, so Damian qualifies easily. Strictly better than trust-paid rent, with a dignity dividend on top.

options.text: Keep the current arrangement — trust pays the landlord, the PMV reduction is capped and predictable, and adding another account adds complexity and a new failure point.
options.outcome: Nothing breaks. But Damian quietly forfeits about $4,200 a year his peers in better-administered trusts would keep, and the simplicity you preserved was mostly yours, not his.
options.explanation: Status quo bias dressed as prudence. The current arrangement IS lawful and stable — that's what makes this answer tempting — and complexity is a real consideration in trust administration. It's inferior because the ABLE route eliminates a known, quantifiable monthly loss at the cost of one well-understood account with modest administrative burden. A prudent administrator weighs cost against benefit; here the benefit is large, recurring, and nearly risk-free. Leaving it unclaimed serves the trustee's convenience, not the beneficiary.

options.text: Open the ABLE account in Tanya's name instead — she handles money better than Damian does, and his benefits can't be touched by an account he doesn't legally own.
options.outcome: An account in Tanya's name is just Tanya's money — SNT distributions into it are distributions to a third party, breaching the trust's sole-benefit requirement, and none of ABLE's protections apply to Damian at all.
options.explanation: ABLE accounts belong to the eligible individual with the disability — that ownership is what makes the tax treatment and benefits exclusions work. Routing first-party SNT funds into a parent's personal account violates the sole-benefit rule at the heart of (d)(4)(A) trusts and constitutes a distribution to someone other than the beneficiary: misappropriation with extra steps, however good the intentions. If Damian needs decision support, ABLE programs allow authorized legal representatives — the answer is structure, never diversion.

stages.narrative: The corpus has a problem of its own: just over $1 million sits in the trust's checking account earning nothing while inflation works on it nightly. This is a court-supervised SNT — the court approved its creation and reviews your accountings — and Damian's life expectancy means this money must work for five more decades.
stages.prompt: How do you invest a court-supervised special needs trust?

options.text: Hire a qualified advisor to build a diversified plan for the 50-year horizon, seek court approval, and keep documented quarterly oversight.
options.outcome: The court approves a diversified portfolio with a cash reserve for two years of distributions. Your quarterly advisor reviews go in the file, and the corpus starts compounding toward the decades it must cover.
options.explanation: Court-supervised SNTs operate under statutory investment restrictions: without a further court order, investments are limited to a conservative list — U.S. and California obligations of five years or less, securities on established exchanges, certain money market funds, and the like. The prudent investor rule demands more for a 26-year-old: portfolio-as-a-whole thinking, diversification, and attention to liquidity, taxes, risk tolerance, and unique circumstances. The solution is to bring the court a professionally built plan and get the order — then supervise the professional, since oversight duty never delegates away.

options.text: Invest the corpus in a ladder of U.S. Treasury obligations of five years or less — squarely on the authorized list, no petition needed, principal essentially guaranteed.
options.outcome: The money is safe, compliant, and slowly losing the only race that matters: a 50-year liability stream versus Treasury yields. Five years on, the real value of Damian's safety net has measurably eroded.
options.explanation: This answer knows the law — short federal obligations are on the authorized list, and skipping the petition saves time and fees — which is exactly its trap. It's inferior because compliance with the default list isn't the same as prudence for this beneficiary: the prudent investor rule evaluates the portfolio against the trust's actual purposes, and a half-century horizon demands growth assets that the default list can't adequately supply. The statute provides a floor and a procedure to rise above it; the prudent trustee uses both.

options.text: Leave the funds sitting in the trust's checking account — no investment can lose money that was never invested, and no court faults a trustee for taking zero risk.
options.outcome: Three accountings later, the court examiner asks why a million dollars has sat uninvested through years of inflation. 'Zero risk' turns out to be a guaranteed-loss strategy the court can quantify to the dollar.
options.explanation: A trustee has an affirmative duty to make trust property productive; idle cash at scale is itself an imprudent investment decision, not the absence of one. Inflation versus a 50-year horizon makes the loss certain rather than speculative — courts can and do surcharge trustees for prolonged failure to invest. Inaction is a choice, and the prudent investor rule judges it like any other.

stages.narrative: Tanya schedules a meeting and arrives with a list. The family van is dying, and Damian's wheelchair barely fits — she wants the trust to buy a $45,000 accessible van, titled to her 'since I do all the driving.' Also on the list: a family trip to Hawaii, all five of them, 'because Damian's therapist said travel would be good for him.' She's been his unpaid caregiver for two years, and her exhaustion is real.
stages.prompt: An accessible van, a family vacation, and a first-party trust bound to Damian's sole benefit. What do you approve?

options.text: Buy the accessible van as a trust asset with use controls; cover Damian's Hawaii costs and one necessary caregiver's; decline the rest of the family.
options.outcome: The van — titled to the trust, insured, mileage-logged — changes Damian's weekly life. He and Tanya go to Hawaii with his costs and hers as attending caregiver covered; the siblings pay their own way. Nobody is thrilled; everybody is treated lawfully.
options.explanation: A first-party SNT permits payments for non-beneficiaries only when their services are necessary for the beneficiary — which is precisely what an attending caregiver's travel is, and what siblings' vacation tickets are not. The accessible van is a classic allowable expenditure when structured for the beneficiary: held as a trust asset with documented use controls, not gifted into a family member's name. This answer threads the actual rule: generous where the trust may be, firm where it may not.

options.text: Decline both requests — the safest reading of the sole-benefit rule is that money leaving the trust toward a family member's hands is money at risk.
options.outcome: The trust stays pristine. Damian keeps missing appointments the dying van can't make, the therapist's travel recommendation goes nowhere, and Tanya — the unpaid infrastructure of Damian's whole life — gets her first lesson in what the trust won't do for the person doing everything.
options.explanation: Caution about family-adjacent distributions is well-founded — overreach in exactly this category is how trustees get surcharged, which makes blanket denial feel safe. It's inferior because the sole-benefit rule permits, not just forbids: transportation and recreation for the beneficiary are quintessential proper purposes, and necessary-caregiver expenses are expressly allowable. A trustee who denies what the trust exists to provide hasn't protected the beneficiary — they've just protected themselves at his expense.

options.text: Use the requests to settle an old debt: pay Tanya $30,000 for two years of past caregiving, papered as back wages, with the van and the trip rolled into the package.
options.outcome: A retroactive $30,000 payment to the trustee's main family contact, invented after the fact with no care agreement, no court approval, and no payroll records, reads to the examiner exactly like what it is — and the surcharge motion writes itself.
options.explanation: Family caregivers CAN be compensated from an SNT — prospectively, under a written care agreement at fair market rates, with court approval and proper payroll treatment. Conjuring retroactive 'wages' to satisfy a relative converts trust assets to a third party with paperwork as disguise; it risks gift treatment, benefits consequences, tax exposure, and a finding of breach. And remember whose money this ultimately protects: at Damian's death the state's Medi-Cal payback claim comes first — every improper dollar out is a dollar the trustee may personally restore.

epilogues.triumph: At the third annual accounting, the judge pauses on the record: benefits intact, corpus growing under an approved plan, an ABLE account returning $4,200 a year to the beneficiary, and a young man living in his own apartment with a van that gets him everywhere. 'This,' the court says to a packed calendar, 'is what these trusts are for.' The settlement bar takes note, and your SNT practice doubles within the year.
epilogues.solid: Damian's benefits survived and the trust is sound — the fundamentals held. A few opportunities arrived late or not at all, and the accounting drew questions you'd rather not have answered. But the corpus is invested, the apartment is his, and Tanya has stopped bracing for disaster. Competent work, with room above it.
epilogues.shaky: The benefits survived, barely — an overpayment here, a suspended check there, each one traceable to a distribution decision made faster than it was thought through. The court approves your accounting with a written reminder of the sole-benefit rule and orders annual rather than biennial review. Tanya has started taking notes in your meetings.
epilogues.disaster: Damian's SSI is gone, his Medi-Cal is in appeals, and the trust is paying $3,100 a month for medication that used to be covered. The court finds multiple breaches of the sole-benefit rule, surcharges you personally, and appoints a successor trustee — who discovers the state's payback claim now shadows a corpus your decisions diminished. The Bureau's letter arrives the following week.

title: The Sergeant's Ledger
tagline: Three agencies, two spouses, one shrinking pot of money — and every rule is different.

client.name: Earl Washington
client.snapshot: A Vietnam-era Army sergeant turned union electrician, now contending with Parkinson's disease and advancing dementia. He lives at home with Mae, his wife of 52 years, on Social Security, a small pension, and a brokerage account he hasn't touched since the nineties. Mae is sharp, scared, and determined not to lose the house.

intro: Mae Washington serves you coffee in a kitchen where every bill is opened, sorted, and increasingly unpayable. You were appointed conservator of Earl's estate last month after his Parkinson's-related dementia made him prey for a phone scammer who nearly emptied the checking account. The math on the table is stark: Earl needs growing levels of care, the income doesn't cover it, and Mae whispers her real terror while Earl dozes — 'They take the house, don't they? When the nursing home comes, they take everything.' Between Social Security, the VA, Medicare, Medi-Cal, and an old brokerage account stuffed with one stock, every dollar in Earl's life answers to a different rulebook. Your job is to know all of them.

stages.narrative: First task: take control of the income. Earl's Social Security — $2,840 a month — direct-deposits into the joint account the scammer nearly drained. You have certified Letters of Conservatorship in your bag and a branch appointment this afternoon.
stages.prompt: How do you take control of Earl's Social Security benefits?

options.text: Apply to SSA to be Earl's representative payee, then receive the benefits into a titled account and account to SSA.
options.outcome: SSA processes your payee application and the benefits begin flowing to a dedicated payee account. The conservatorship and payee records run on parallel tracks, each agency getting exactly the accounting its rules require.
options.explanation: Social Security benefits answer to federal law, not the probate court: a conservatorship Letters packet, however certified, does not give you authority over SSA payments. The representative payee is SSA's own appointment, with its own application, its own duty to use funds for the beneficiary's current needs, and its own accounting directly to SSA. A professional fiduciary commonly wears both hats — conservator and payee — but they are separate offices earned through separate doors.

options.text: Present your certified Letters at the bank and redirect the direct deposit into your new conservatorship account — the court's order covers all of Earl's assets and income.
options.outcome: The bank, seeing valid Letters, makes the change. Months later an SSA review flags that benefits are being managed by someone the agency never appointed, freezing the deposits while your after-the-fact payee application crawls through processing.
options.explanation: This is the intuitive move — Letters genuinely do reach Earl's other income and the bank may well honor them — which is exactly why it's the classic trap. It's inferior because SSA does not recognize state-court conservatorship authority over its benefits: managing Social Security requires SSA's own representative payee appointment, and skipping it leaves you administering federal benefits without federal authority. The funds end up in the right place by the wrong door, and the agency eventually checks the door.

options.text: Leave the direct deposit where it is and let Mae keep managing the Social Security informally, since she's capable and it spares the family another change.
options.outcome: The arrangement that nearly lost $40,000 to a phone scammer continues unchanged. When the next 'grandson in trouble' call gets through to Earl, the conservatorship you were appointed to run has protected nothing.
options.explanation: The conservatorship exists because the informal arrangement failed: Earl was scammed through exactly this account. Leaving benefits outside your control abdicates the duty to marshal and protect income — and Mae, however capable, holds no legal authority over Earl's benefits either. Sympathy for a spouse's routine cannot substitute for the protective structure the court ordered you to build.

stages.narrative: Earl needs daily help with bathing, dressing, and medication — the kind of regular aid-and-attendance that a Vietnam-era veteran's service may have earned him. Mae produces a cigar box of Army papers, and there it is: his DD214. The pension math is tight: the household's net worth sits just under the VA's limit, and his son Curtis 'knows a guy who helps vets qualify, for a cut.'
stages.prompt: How do you pursue VA benefits for Earl?

options.text: Apply for needs-based pension with Aid and Attendance through an accredited VSO, which charges nothing, after verifying net worth and making no transfers.
options.outcome: The accredited VSO builds the file, the net worth verification clears the limit with documentation to prove it, and months later Earl's award letter arrives — roughly $2,300 a month in tax-free Aid and Attendance toward his daily care.
options.explanation: Every VA application starts with the DD214. Aid and Attendance is the top tier of the needs-based pension for wartime-era veterans needing help with daily living, subject to a net worth test (about $163,699 including annual income, excluding the residence and vehicle). Applications go through VA-accredited representatives — VSOs cannot charge for this service — and the VA's 3-year lookback on gifts and below-market transfers, with penalties up to five years of ineligibility, makes pre-application asset shuffling dangerous. Free, accredited, documented: that's the whole formula.

options.text: File the application yourself directly with the VA — you're the conservator, the forms are public, and skipping the intermediary gets the claim moving immediately.
options.outcome: The claim is filed fast — and comes back ten weeks later for development: a missing physician's aid-and-attendance examination form and an incomplete net worth disclosure an experienced representative would have caught at intake. The do-it-yourself head start becomes a four-month detour.
options.explanation: Nothing prohibits filing directly, and a conservator taking initiative is acting within their role — that's the appeal. It's inferior because VA claims are a specialized practice where accredited VSOs navigate the medical evidence requirements, net worth presentation, and effective-date strategy at zero cost to the estate. When free expert help exists and the downside of error is months of delayed care funding, the prudent fiduciary consults the professional — the same principle that says hire the probate-experienced realtor, applied to benefits.

options.text: Engage Curtis's contact, a self-described 'veterans benefits consultant' who charges 15% of the first year's award but flatly guarantees that Earl will qualify.
options.outcome: Your attorney flags it in one phone call: charging veterans for application preparation violates federal law, the 'guarantee' is a sales line, and the consultant's signature move — 'repositioning assets' to qualify — is the exact transfer behavior the lookback punishes.
options.explanation: Federal law prohibits charging fees to prepare and file VA benefit applications — only VA-accredited representatives may assist, and VSOs do it free. The paid-consultant industry that targets aging veterans survives on families who don't know this, and its asset-repositioning tactics routinely trigger lookback penalties that cost more than the consultant's fee. A fiduciary's job is to be the person in the room who knows the free, lawful channel exists.

stages.narrative: Earl falls in the bathroom and spends four days at the hospital. The discharge planner is brisk and kind: 'We're recommending skilled nursing for rehab — Medicare will cover it.' Mae exhales for the first time in days. But riding down in the elevator, you reread the paperwork: Earl's four days are coded 'observation status.'
stages.prompt: The discharge planner says Medicare will cover the SNF stay. Do you trust it?

options.text: Verify his status before discharge, since observation days don't count toward the three-day inpatient requirement, and push for reclassification now.
options.outcome: Pressed for a physician review, the hospital reclassifies two of the days; with an extended stay Earl crosses the three-day inpatient threshold, and his rehab is covered — 20 days at no cost, a copay after. You note day 100 on your calendar anyway: nothing about that deadline will surprise this estate.
options.explanation: The observation-status trap is the most tested Medicare distinction there is: SNF coverage requires a three-day qualifying INPATIENT stay, and observation days — however identical the bed and the bracelet — do not count. Catching the coding before discharge, while reclassification and appeal are still live options, is worth tens of thousands of dollars. And the benefit itself has edges to plan around: 100% for the first 20 SNF days, a daily copay for days 21 through 100, and zero Medicare coverage beyond day 100.

options.text: Proceed with the SNF placement now — Earl genuinely needs the rehab — and contest the billing afterward if Medicare denies the claim.
options.outcome: Earl gets his rehab without delay. The denial arrives in week three — no qualifying inpatient stay — and the estate is suddenly fighting an after-the-fact appeal with discharge-era evidence nobody preserved, while SNF charges accrue at private rates.
options.explanation: Prioritizing Earl's medical need over paperwork is the right instinct — care first is usually sound fiduciary thinking, which makes this answer feel responsible. It's inferior because the status question costs nothing to verify before discharge, when reclassification is realistic and evidence is fresh, while post-denial appeals are slow and usually fail. There was no actual trade-off between care and verification here: both were available, and the prudent fiduciary takes both.

options.text: Plan on Medicare carrying Earl's nursing home costs over the long term — he's fully enrolled in Parts A and B, and skilled nursing is exactly what Part A covers.
options.outcome: Whatever rehab coverage exists ends within weeks of admission. Nobody has run the Medi-Cal numbers, nobody has protected Mae's position, and the first private-pay invoice — north of $12,000 — lands on a household with no plan.
options.explanation: Medicare is acute-care insurance, not long-term care insurance: it covers skilled REHABILITATION (capped at 100 days, with copays after day 20) and never custodial care — the help with bathing, dressing, and supervision that is precisely what dementia patients need most. Long-term custodial coverage is Medi-Cal's territory, with its own eligibility planning that takes time. A fiduciary who confuses the two programs discovers the difference on an invoice.

stages.narrative: Rehab ends, and the care conference delivers the verdict everyone feared: Earl can't safely come home. He needs long-term skilled nursing — $11,500 a month, indefinitely. Mae sits across from you that evening with the question she's been carrying since your first cup of coffee: 'Do I lose the house? Do I lose everything?'
stages.prompt: How do you plan for long-term care costs while protecting Mae?

options.text: Hire an elder law attorney to build the Medi-Cal plan: the home is exempt for Mae, the CSRA protects $162,660, and the lookback gets every step vetted.
options.outcome: The plan comes together: house exempt and untouched, Mae's protected resources documented to the dollar, Earl's Medi-Cal application filed clean. The night you walk Mae through it, she cries with relief — she keeps the house, the car, and enough to live on. The system, navigated correctly, was never going to take everything.
options.explanation: This is exactly the situation Medi-Cal's spousal impoverishment protections exist for: the principal residence is exempt — never rush to sell it — and the CSRA lets the community spouse retain $162,660 (2026) beyond exempt assets, while the institutionalized spouse's income goes to share of cost less a $35 monthly personal needs allowance. The terrain shifted recently — the $130,000 resource limit and a 30-month transfer lookback both returned effective 2026 — which is precisely why specialist counsel plus court approval for plan steps is the prudent fiduciary's path. Consulting professionals on matters this consequential isn't delegation of duty; it is the duty.

options.text: Begin converting countable assets to exempt ones now — prepay irrevocable burial plans, finish the deferred home repairs, replace the failing car — spending down toward eligibility before you file.
options.outcome: Each conversion is individually legitimate, but sequenced by instinct rather than analysis: one purchase needed court approval you didn't seek, the timing muddied a clean eligibility date, and the elder law attorney you eventually hire spends billable hours untangling moves she'd have ordered differently.
options.explanation: These are real Medi-Cal planning techniques — irrevocable burial plans of any amount, home maintenance, and one vehicle are all exempt, and converting countable to exempt assets is the legitimate core of spend-down strategy. It's inferior as a first move because technique without strategy is how planning errors happen: eligibility timing, the reinstated lookback, CSRA optimization, and the conservatorship's court approval requirements all interact, and the sequence matters. Right tools, wrong order, no architect — competent fiduciaries get the plan before executing it.

options.text: Move the brokerage account into Curtis's name before you file the Medi-Cal application — once it's out of Earl's name it can't be counted, and the family keeps what the nursing home would otherwise consume entirely.
options.outcome: The transfer lands squarely in the reinstated lookback, generating a penalty period of Medi-Cal ineligibility precisely when Earl needs coverage — and the court learns its conservator moved six figures to an heir without authorization. The surcharge hearing and the eligibility appeal run concurrently.
options.explanation: Asset-hiding is the move every agency is built to catch: nursing home Medi-Cal's 30-month lookback resumed January 1, 2026, and uncompensated transfers generate ineligibility penalties scaled to the amount moved — the 'protection' creates the exact coverage gap it was meant to prevent. Layered on top: a conservator making unauthorized transfers of estate assets to a family member commits a textbook breach, personally surchargeable. Lawful Medi-Cal planning operates through exemptions and allowances in daylight; it never requires hiding anything.

stages.narrative: The long-term picture stabilizes, but the monthly ledger doesn't: even with Social Security, the pension, and the new Aid and Attendance award, the household runs $1,400 short every month between Earl's share of cost and Mae's living expenses. The gap has to come from somewhere, on purpose.
stages.prompt: How do you manage the ongoing shortfall?

options.text: Build a written plan: document income and expenses, set a sequence tapping depreciating assets first while sparing the exempt home, and reflect it in your accountings.
options.outcome: The plan funds the gap deliberately: the unused second car and a storage unit of depreciating equipment go first, a modest reserve is established, and every accounting you file shows the court an estate being steered rather than drained. When Earl's care needs spike a year later, the contingency line already exists.
options.explanation: A budget and financial plan addressing immediate needs, future needs, and contingencies is a core conservator duty — the managed estate differs from the dwindling one precisely in having a liquidation sequence. Sound sequencing taps depreciating assets first (they lose value while you wait), protects exempt and appreciating assets, and keeps the strategy visible to the court through your accountings. Asset-poor trajectories are survivable when planned; the same numbers without a plan become an emergency on a schedule.

options.text: Cover the shortfall by drawing $1,400 from the brokerage account each month — the money exists for exactly this, and a standing monthly transfer is simple and transparent.
options.outcome: The bills get paid and the records stay clean, but the drawdown runs on autopilot: nobody has asked which assets should fund the gap, what the depletion curve looks like, or what happens when care costs rise. Eighteen months in, the examiner asks for the long-term plan — and there isn't one to show.
options.explanation: Using estate assets for the conservatee's support is legitimate — that's what the estate is for — and the transparency of a regular documented draw makes this feel responsible. It's inferior because a recurring transfer is a payment method, not a plan: it doesn't sequence which assets to consume first, doesn't account for the brokerage's tax and investment characteristics, and doesn't model the runway. The duty is to manage the estate's trajectory, not merely to keep current bills paid while the horizon goes unexamined.

options.text: Fold Mae's community property assets into your conservatorship budget and manage the household's entire finances yourself — one ledger, one manager, and no coverage gaps.
options.outcome: Mae's attorney sends a letter that your own attorney reads aloud, slowly: the conservator has asserted control over assets belonging to a capable spouse with the exclusive legal right to manage them. The apology and the unwinding both go in the court file.
options.explanation: When a conservatee has a capable spouse, that spouse holds the EXCLUSIVE right to manage the community property — it doesn't enter the conservatorship estate without her consent, and only Earl's separate property is automatically yours to manage.
