Mae is not a ward; she is a legally capable co-owner. Coordinating budgets with her is good practice; absorbing her property into your authority is an overreach the law specifically forbids.

stages.narrative: Last item in the ledger: the brokerage account Earl hasn't touched since the nineties — $410,000, with 78% of it in a single technology stock he bought as a young electrician because he 'liked their soldering irons.' The position is up four-thousand percent. It is also one earnings call away from being the estate's biggest problem.
stages.prompt: What do you do with a concentrated stock position you inherited as conservator?

options.text: Hire an advisor to design a whole-portfolio diversification plan weighing the gains, liquidity, and life expectancy, get court approval, and supervise quarterly.
options.outcome: The court approves a staged diversification that manages the tax hit across two years while building the liquidity Earl's care demands. When the tech stock drops 30% the following spring, the estate's exposure is a fraction of what it was — and your quarterly oversight memos are already in the file.
options.explanation: The prudent investor rule judges the portfolio as a whole and demands diversification — a 78% single-stock concentration fails that standard regardless of how brilliantly the position has performed, because past gains are not a risk management strategy. The execution path matters equally: changing investments requires prior court approval in a conservatorship, securities expertise calls for a qualified professional rather than self-management, and hiring the advisor never delegates away your duty — ongoing oversight with quarterly review is the standard. Plan, approve, execute, supervise: all four, in order.

options.text: Retain the position — keeping existing assets needs no court approval, the stock has been a forty-year winner, and selling triggers an enormous capital gains bill the estate can ill afford.
options.outcome: Every individual point holds up — until the concentration question is asked directly at your accounting hearing, and 'it always went up before' is the only answer in the file. The court orders an investment review; the review reaches the obvious conclusion; you've arrived at diversification anyway, a year late and minus the court's confidence.
options.explanation: This answer is armored in true facts — retention of existing assets genuinely requires no court approval, the gains tax is real, and the track record is spectacular — which makes it the most seductive wrong-ish answer in the case. It's inferior because the prudent investor rule evaluates risk prospectively and portfolio-wide: 78% in one issuer is an unacceptable concentration for an estate that must fund years of care, and tax cost is a factor to manage within a diversification plan, not a reason to forgo one. 'No approval needed to do nothing' describes your procedural position, not your fiduciary duty.

options.text: Move the account to your brother-in-law's advisory firm — he's offered the estate a discounted fee schedule, and he pays you referral consideration on the accounts you bring in.
options.outcome: The referral arrangement surfaces in your accounting review, and everything after that happens quickly: the court voids the engagement, orders the consideration disgorged, and refers the matter to the Bureau — where 'discounted fees for the estate' impresses no one.
options.explanation: This is self-dealing with a family-conflict garnish: receiving personal consideration from a client transaction is flatly prohibited — the same principle that bars keeping credit card miles from client purchases, scaled up — and steering estate business to family requires disclosure and court approval even without a kickback. The indirect conflict rule exists because professionals you select owe their loyalty to the client, not to your household's income. No fee discount launders a fiduciary's personal profit from the estate's business; this is the conflict-of-interest trifecta, and it is license-ending.

epilogues.triumph: A year on, the ledger balances: Aid and Attendance flowing, Medi-Cal covering Earl's care with the house and Mae's CSRA fully protected, the portfolio diversified under court order, and accountings the examiner approves without a single question. Mae brings cookies to your office every Veterans Day. The probate judge has started describing complex multi-benefit estates as 'a case for someone like the conservator in Washington.'
epilogues.solid: The major pieces landed — benefits secured, house protected, Earl's care funded — though the file shows some detours: a denied claim here, a late plan there. The court approves your accountings with minor questions, Mae sleeps at night, and you keep a one-page checklist now, taped above your desk: SSA, VA, Medicare, Medi-Cal — four agencies, four rulebooks, no assumptions.
epilogues.shaky: Earl's care is funded, but the route there cost real money — a coverage denial that verification would have caught, a penalty period that planning would have avoided. The court approves your accounting with written concerns and orders supplemental reporting on the estate's diminished reserves. Mae is polite at your meetings now, and brings her own notepad.
epilogues.disaster: The losses compound on paper the court reads aloud: unauthorized transfers, a lookback penalty during the months Earl most needed coverage, an estate bled by decisions no one approved. You are surcharged, removed, and reported to the Bureau — and the successor conservator's first filing itemizes, with citations, everything that should have happened instead. Mae doesn't look at you as you leave the courtroom.

title: The Price of Diligence
tagline: Every hour you bill, somebody is watching the meter.

client.name: Theodore "Teddy" Okafor
client.snapshot: Retired aerospace machinist from Long Beach who suffered a major stroke in March. His estate — a paid-off house, a pension, and about $640,000 in savings — needs a steady hand. His daughter Adaeze is a sharp-eyed CPA who reads every document twice.

intro: You sign the Oath of Office on a gray Tuesday morning, and by Friday you are elbow-deep in Teddy Okafor's life: a stack of unopened mail, a pension check that needs redirecting, and a probate referee who hasn't returned your call about the appraisal. Your own practice is young, and the office rent doesn't wait for anyone. Adaeze, Teddy's daughter, emails you a spreadsheet of questions about your hourly rate before you've even finished marshaling the accounts. You can already tell: in this case, your fees will be examined under a magnifying glass.

stages.narrative: Six weeks after your appointment, you've logged more than forty hours — securing the house, redirecting income, untangling an old annuity. Your office manager flags a cash-flow crunch and suggests requesting your fees now. The Inventory & Appraisal is still sitting with the probate referee, unfiled.
stages.prompt: When and how do you seek your first compensation from Teddy's estate?

options.text: Keep careful time records, press the referee, and file no fee request until the 90 days have run and the I&A is on file.
options.outcome: You calendar both dates, nudge the referee weekly, and the I&A gets filed in week eleven. Your time records are airtight when the window finally opens.
options.explanation: A conservator cannot request fees until 90 days after appointment AND the Inventory & Appraisal has been filed. The I&A exists partly so the court can measure your requested fees against the actual size of the estate. Waiting while documenting thoroughly is exactly what the rule contemplates.

options.text: Have your attorney file the fee petition now, but deliberately set the hearing date for after the 90-day mark so the court won't actually rule until the waiting period has fully run.
options.outcome: The clerk accepts the filing, but the probate examiner's notes flag the petition as premature, and your attorney has to file a supplement once the I&A lands.
options.explanation: This feels like clever lawyering, but the rule bars REQUESTING fees before 90 days have run and the I&A is filed — not merely receiving them. Filing early puts a defective request on record and asks the court to evaluate fees before it can see the estate's appraised value. Preparing the petition in advance is fine; filing it is not.

options.text: Move a modest $2,500 draw from the conservatorship account into your office account now, planning to ask the court for retroactive approval at the first accounting.
options.outcome: The withdrawal sits on the bank statement like a flare. When the first accounting is filed, the court demands an explanation and orders the funds returned with interest.
options.explanation: The Probate Code requires court approval BEFORE fees are paid. Paying yourself first and asking forgiveness later is self-dealing with estate funds — grounds for surcharge, removal, and a report to the Professional Fiduciaries Bureau, no matter how reasonable the underlying hours were.

stages.narrative: Ninety days pass and the I&A is filed: a $642,000 estate. As you assemble your first fee petition, you notice your hours include routine bill-paying and mail-sorting your assistant performed, plus three hours you personally spent learning your new case-management software.
stages.prompt: How do you structure the billing in the fee petition?

options.text: Bill your professional rate only for work needing judgment, bill clerical tasks at your assistant's rate, and write off your own training.
options.outcome: The petition reads cleanly: tiered rates, every entry tied to a necessary task. The probate examiner's notes come back with zero fee objections.
options.explanation: The three-part reasonableness test asks: (1) was the activity necessary, (2) is the rate reasonable, and (3) are different rates used for different skill levels? Clerical work billed at a professional rate fails part three, and your own training benefits you, not Teddy — under the NGA fee factors, compensable work must produce a benefit to the client.

options.text: Bill every hour at your full professional rate, but then apply a voluntary 15% courtesy discount to the grand total as a visible show of good faith toward the estate.
options.outcome: The court approves a reduced amount anyway, and the judge remarks that she'd rather see rates matched to tasks than an arbitrary haircut.
options.explanation: A blanket discount looks generous, but it is not a substitute for the reasonableness test, which evaluates rate against skill level activity by activity. A flat reduction still bills clerical work at professional rates — it just hides the problem inside an average. Defensible, but analytically inferior to tiered billing.

options.text: Round each task up to the nearest half hour and reconstruct time estimates from memory for the two weeks you forgot to log your hours contemporaneously.
options.outcome: Adaeze, the CPA, cross-references your invoice against bank timestamps and facility visit logs — and files a detailed objection alleging inflated billing.
options.explanation: Systematic rounding-up and reconstructed estimates presented as actual time are misrepresentations to the court. A fiduciary's fee petition is a sworn submission; padding it is a breach of the duty of honesty that invites surcharge, fee denial, and Bureau discipline. Unlogged time is the fiduciary's loss, not the estate's.

stages.narrative: Your draft invoice includes line items for photocopies, postage, mileage to Teddy's local bank, and your secretary's time preparing mailings. Your attorney looks at the draft and raises an eyebrow without saying a word.
stages.prompt: What do you do with these charges?

options.text: Strike them — copies, postage, local travel, and secretarial time are overhead already built into your hourly rate.
options.outcome: The cleaned-up invoice survives Adaeze's line-by-line review without a single overhead objection.
options.explanation: Ordinary overhead — copying, postage, local travel, secretarial time — is considered part of the fiduciary's compensation, not a reimbursable estate expense. Your hourly rate is presumed to absorb the cost of running your office. Passing overhead through as line items effectively double-bills the conservatee.

options.text: Leave the items on the invoice but flag them prominently in the petition and ask the court itself to decide whether each one is properly chargeable to the estate.
options.outcome: The judge strikes the items and adds, not unkindly, that she expects licensed professionals to know the difference between overhead and billable work.
options.explanation: Transparency is a virtue, but punting a settled question to the judge is not. The rule that routine overhead is part of compensation is well established; a professional fiduciary is expected to apply it, not litigate it. You've spent court time and estate money confirming something you should have known.

options.text: Reclassify the items as 'case administration' hours billed at your assistant's lower rate, so that they read on the petition as services performed rather than as costs.
options.outcome: The examiner notices that 'case administration' time correlates suspiciously with postage dates and asks pointed questions at the hearing.
options.explanation: Relabeling overhead as billable time doesn't change what it is — it disguises it. Dressed-up cost recovery is worse than the original error because it adds an element of concealment to a charge that was improper to begin with.

stages.narrative: Your fee petition is ready. Teddy cannot meaningfully review an invoice anymore, and Adaeze has demanded 'full detail on every penny.' Her brother Chuka, who lives in Atlanta and rarely calls, is also an heir and notice party.
stages.prompt: How do you handle distribution of your invoices and the opportunity to object?

options.text: Serve detailed invoices on the proper parties — Teddy's counsel, Adaeze, and Chuka — with about 20 days to object before the hearing.
options.outcome: Adaeze sends back three questions, you answer them with backup documentation, and the objection window closes quietly.
options.explanation: Fee practice requires invoices showing billable activity and hours, sent to the appropriate parties — which means beneficiaries and the client's representatives once the client is incapacitated — with a meaningful period to object, typically 20 days. Affirmative, detailed disclosure before the hearing is what makes court approval an informed act rather than a rubber stamp.

options.text: File the detailed invoices with the court as exhibits to the petition, and let any interested party who wishes to review them simply do so in the public court file.
options.outcome: Chuka, who never checks the court docket, learns the amount of your fees for the first time at the hearing and asks the judge for a continuance to review them.
options.explanation: Filing detail with the court satisfies the letter of disclosure but not its purpose. The standard is to SEND invoices to the appropriate parties and give them a real chance to object — passive availability in a court file shifts the burden onto family members to discover what you should have delivered. It risks continuances and the appearance of burying detail.

options.text: Serve everyone except Adaeze, reasoning that her open hostility makes giving her advance notice counterproductive to running a smooth, efficient hearing.
options.outcome: Adaeze appears at the hearing anyway, notice defect in hand, and the judge vacates the fee order and orders re-service on all parties.
options.explanation: Deliberately omitting an interested party from notice because she is likely to object is a due-process violation, not a litigation tactic. The objection period exists precisely FOR the skeptics. Selective notice can void the resulting order and marks you, in the court's eyes, as a fiduciary who manages oversight rather than submits to it.

stages.narrative: The court approves your fees and authorizes a periodic payment arrangement going forward. Six months later, Teddy's condition worsens and he moves to memory care at $9,000 a month. Projections now show the estate depleting in about six years.
stages.prompt: What do you do about your ongoing periodic fee draws?

options.text: Reassess under the NGA factors, trim your periodic draws to fit Teddy's future needs, and flag the change to the court.
options.outcome: Your report candidly projects the estate's runway and shows your fees shrinking as Teddy's care costs grow. The judge initials the margin: 'Noted, and appreciated.'
options.explanation: The NGA fee factors require weighing the client's anticipated future needs and income, not just the work performed. When care costs threaten the estate's sufficiency, a fiduciary acting in the client's best interest adjusts compensation proactively. Periodic payments must also never exceed projected total fees — and the projection just changed.

options.text: Continue the court-authorized draws exactly as they are — the court approved this precise arrangement, your workload hasn't dropped, and nothing in the order requires you to revisit it now.
options.outcome: Nothing improper appears on the books, but at the next accounting the judge asks why your fee level never responded to Teddy's changed circumstances — and you don't have a great answer.
options.explanation: Relying on the existing order is defensible — the payments are authorized and the work is real. But an order is not a blank check against changed circumstances. The NGA factors demand a forward look at the client's needs; the BEST course recognizes that the conservatee's runway now competes directly with your compensation and adjusts before being asked.

options.text: Take a lump-sum advance against several future years of your anticipated fees right now, while the funds in the depleting estate are still actually there to cover it.
options.outcome: The advance shows up at the next accounting as a five-figure unauthorized distribution. The court surcharges you and the surety gets a phone call.
options.explanation: You cannot pay yourself periodic fees exceeding projected total fees, and you cannot take ANY fee without prior court approval — an 'advance' against unearned future work fails both rules at once. Extracting estate funds ahead of need, from a depleting estate, is the textbook posture of fiduciary self-dealing: surcharge, removal, and license discipline territory.

stages.narrative: At the first accounting, Adaeze files a formal written objection: your fees are excessive, and the work — she argues — benefited your practice, not her father. Judge Okada sets a contested hearing and looks at you over her glasses as she does it.
stages.prompt: How do you respond to the fee objection?

options.text: File a verified response backed by your records, tie each task to its benefit to Teddy, offer Adaeze's counsel full access, and let the court rule.
options.outcome: Confronted with organized, contemporaneous records, Adaeze's counsel withdraws half the objection before the hearing. Judge Okada approves your fees with a minor reduction and a comment about 'commendable documentation.'
options.explanation: The fiduciary bears the burden of proving fees are reasonable — necessity, rate, and skill level — and the open-book duty means objectors get access, not stonewalling. Meeting an objection with documentation and transparency, then submitting to the court's judgment, is precisely how the court-supervision system is designed to work.

options.text: Instruct your attorney to negotiate a voluntary fee reduction with Adaeze so that she agrees to withdraw her objection before the contested hearing ever has to happen.
options.outcome: Adaeze accepts a 20% haircut and withdraws. But Judge Okada asks at the hearing why properly earned fees were bargained away — and whether the original petition was inflated to leave room for negotiating.
options.explanation: Settling objections is a legitimate tool and saves the estate litigation costs — that's what makes this attractive. But fees still require court approval on their merits regardless of any private deal, and conceding a discount on properly documented work signals the billing may have been soft. The stronger course is to prove the fees, not to purchase peace.

options.text: Argue to the court that Adaeze's objection is really driven by personal family hostility toward you, and on that basis ask the judge to simply disregard it.
options.outcome: Judge Okada cuts you off: 'Her motives are not the question, counsel. Your fees are.' The hearing goes downhill from there.
options.explanation: Attacking the objector's motives does nothing to carry your burden of proof. The court must independently determine that fees are reasonable; an objection — whatever drives it — simply triggers the scrutiny you must satisfy with evidence. Personalizing a fee dispute reads as deflection and erodes the court's confidence.

epilogues.triumph: Judge Okada approves your final fee petition without a single adjustment and tells the courtroom your billing practices 'should be a template for the panel.' Adaeze — your fiercest auditor — refers her own client's family to your practice. Teddy's estate funds his care to the end, with a cushion to spare.
epilogues.solid: Your fees survive review with modest trims and a few teachable moments. Adaeze remains watchful but no longer adversarial, and Judge Okada signs your accountings without comment — which, from her, is praise.
epilogues.shaky: The court approves your accountings only after continuances, reductions, and one uncomfortable lecture about overhead and objection rights. Adaeze's complaints stop short of formal action, but Judge Okada now examines your filings line by line, and it shows in your calendar.
epilogues.disaster: The court surcharges unauthorized payments, terminates your periodic fee authorization, and appoints a successor conservator for Teddy. A copy of the findings goes to the Professional Fiduciaries Bureau, and you spend the next year explaining this case to an investigator instead of building a practice.

title: Whose Side Are You On?
tagline: Everyone in this family is sure you work for them.

client.name: Rosa Camarillo
client.snapshot: A retired Fresno schoolteacher with mild-to-moderate dementia, a paid-off home, a rental duplex, and about $300,000 in savings. Her daughter Marisol petitioned for the conservatorship; her son Danny drifts in and out of town with money troubles that nobody discusses at dinner.

intro: Rosa Camarillo keeps her teaching awards on the wall and her opinions close at hand, even on the days the dementia blurs the edges. You've just been appointed conservator of her person and estate, and the family is already orbiting you like weather systems: Marisol, the dutiful daughter who filed the petition, calls daily with instructions delivered as suggestions. Danny, the son, calls only when he needs something. Somewhere in the middle is Rosa — your actual client — who told you on your first visit, 'Mija, just don't let them turn me into a referee's whistle.' You intend to keep that promise.

stages.narrative: Marisol corners you after the appointment hearing. 'Let's be clear,' she says, smiling. 'I petitioned. My attorney got you appointed. I'm paying attention to everything. So functionally, you work for me — run decisions by me first.'
stages.prompt: How do you define the relationship?

options.text: Explain warmly but plainly: Rosa is your only client. You'll keep Marisol informed as family, but decisions follow Rosa's interest, not instructions.
options.outcome: Marisol bristles, then respects it. Months later she admits the clarity made it easier to be a daughter instead of a supervisor.
options.explanation: Before taking any case, the fiduciary must identify the client — and in a conservatorship, the client is the conservatee, never the petitioning family member. Client identity determines the duty of loyalty and who is entitled to what information. Setting that boundary on day one, kindly and in plain language, prevents every downstream conflict this misunderstanding breeds.

options.text: Agree to make Marisol your primary point of contact and to walk every major decision past her before you act, while privately reserving the genuine final authority for yourself.
options.outcome: The arrangement works until it doesn't: when you decline Marisol's preferred caregiver, she accuses you of breaking 'our agreement,' and you spend a month untangling expectations you created.
options.explanation: Engaging family closely is good practice — but routinely pre-clearing decisions with one relative functionally positions her as the client and compromises your independence. The difference from the best answer is structural: information flows to family; decision authority answers only to Rosa's best interest and the court. Courtesy briefings, yes; clearance, no.

options.text: Sign the 'family communication agreement' Marisol proposes, committing you in writing to follow her direction on Rosa's care and finances in return for her continued cooperation.
options.outcome: The document surfaces at the first review hearing. The court investigator describes it as 'a contract to subordinate the conservatee's interests,' and the judge orders you to show cause why you should not be removed.
options.explanation: A written commitment to follow a third party's direction is a contractual breach of the duty of undivided loyalty — essentially an agreement to serve someone other than your client. No disclosure cures it. It is the kind of document that ends appointments and triggers Bureau discipline, because it proves the conflict in your own signature.

stages.narrative: A week later, the attorney who represented Marisol in the petition calls with an offer: he'll represent you as conservator at a 'family friendly' discount. 'I know the file cold,' he says. 'Why pay someone new to learn it?'
stages.prompt: Do you hire him?

options.text: Decline in writing, and retain your own independent counsel who had no prior role in the petition or anywhere else in the case.
options.outcome: Your new attorney's first act is spotting an issue petitioner's counsel had glossed over — a loan from Rosa to Marisol that was never documented. Independence pays for itself immediately.
options.explanation: An attorney who represents the petitioner cannot also represent the fiduciary — the petitioner's interests and the conservatee's can collide, and your counsel must answer to your duties alone. The standard practice is to hire separate counsel, and to decline identified conflicts in writing so the record shows you recognized and refused the entanglement.

options.text: Accept the representation, but only after you have obtained a signed written conflict waiver from all of the parties and disclosed the dual relationship openly to the court.
options.outcome: The disclosure draws a frown from the bench. When the undocumented loan to Marisol surfaces, the attorney must withdraw from representing anyone — and the estate pays twice for new counsel to relearn the file.
options.explanation: Waivers and disclosure are the right instincts for many conflicts, which makes this option tempting. But here the conflict is structural: the lawyer's former client (the petitioner) is a person whose conduct you may need to investigate or oppose. The best answer avoids the conflict rather than papering it — separate counsel is the professional norm precisely because cases like Rosa's so often turn against a family member.

options.text: Accept, and quietly use the shared attorney as a convenient back channel to keep Marisol informed about case strategy and the running details of Rosa's finances.
options.outcome: Confidential financial details flow straight to Marisol — and then to Danny, and then into a family group chat. The court investigator's next report reads like an indictment.
options.explanation: This compounds a disqualifying conflict with a confidentiality breach: funneling the conservatee's private information to a family member through dual-role counsel. It violates the duty to determine disclosure by Rosa's preferences and interests, and it weaponizes the very conflict that separate-counsel rules exist to prevent.

stages.narrative: Rosa's low-mileage Buick has to be sold — she can't drive, and insurance is bleeding the estate. Your nephew texts: 'I'll pay whatever the appraisal says, cash.' The same afternoon, your assistant suggests charging estate expenses to your personal rewards card: 'The miles add up, and the estate reimburses anyway.'
stages.prompt: How do you handle the car — and the card?

options.text: Sell the Buick on the open market at arm's length, and pay estate expenses straight from the conservatorship account — no personal cards, no rewards.
options.outcome: The Buick fetches $900 over appraisal from a stranger who saw the listing. Your books show clean, direct payment trails a court examiner could follow blindfolded.
options.explanation: A fiduciary cannot buy or sell property from or to the estate, and cannot receive personal benefits — including credit-card miles — from client transactions. The open market eliminates any question of divided interest, and direct payment from the conservatorship account preserves the separation of funds that the no-personal-benefit rule protects.

options.text: Sell the Buick to your nephew at the independently appraised value, with full written disclosure of your family relationship to him filed with the court for its approval.
options.outcome: The court allows the sale, but the investigator's report notes the relationship, and at the next hearing the judge asks why an open-market sale wasn't attempted first. You don't have a satisfying answer.
options.explanation: Disclosure and a fair price are real safeguards, which is what makes this defensible. But it remains a transaction benefiting your own family when an unconflicted alternative — the open market — was freely available. The discipline of conflict avoidance is choosing the path with NO personal connection when one exists; disclosure mitigates a conflict, it doesn't make it the best option.

options.text: Buy the Buick yourself, paying slightly above the appraised value, on the theory that Rosa nets MORE money this way than any stranger would ever pay her.
options.outcome: The generous price impresses no one. The court voids the sale, orders the car returned, and opens an inquiry into every other transaction you've handled for Rosa.
options.explanation: Self-dealing is prohibited absolutely: the fiduciary cannot purchase property from the estate, period — the Professional Fiduciaries Act and NGA standards bar it regardless of price. The rule is prophylactic; it doesn't ask whether this deal was fair, because a fiduciary negotiating with themself can never be trusted to know. 'I paid extra' is how every self-dealing defense begins.

stages.narrative: Rosa is calmest and happiest in Marisol's care — the agency aides unsettle her, and she's stopped eating well on agency days. Marisol offers to become the paid caregiver at $28 an hour. The going agency rate is $38.
stages.prompt: Can you hire the conservatee's daughter — and if so, how?

options.text: Document the comparison with agencies, and because Rosa does best with Marisol, petition the court BEFORE any pay — disclosed relationship, fair terms, supervision plan.
options.outcome: The court approves the arrangement. Rosa's appetite returns, the cost is below agency rates, and the order means nobody can later paint the hire as a backroom family deal.
options.explanation: Family members may be hired only when the relationship is fully disclosed to the court, the terms beat or match independent alternatives in the conservatee's best interest, and the services are competently performed under supervision — and you cannot employ family without court approval. Here the person-centered facts (Rosa thrives with Marisol, at lower cost) genuinely support the hire, so the right move is the approved, supervised version of it.

options.text: Avoid the family-hire problem entirely by retaining an independent agency instead, accepting that Rosa does measurably worse with agency staff than she does with her own daughter.
options.outcome: Your file is conflict-free and the court asks no questions — but Rosa keeps losing weight on agency days, and her quality of life quietly erodes for the sake of your clean paperwork.
options.explanation: Avoiding conflicts is usually sound instinct, which makes this attractive. But the family-hire rules exist precisely because sometimes a relative IS the best care — the law permits it with disclosure, best-interest terms, and court approval. Choosing administrative comfort over Rosa's demonstrated wellbeing puts your risk management above person-centered practice. The conservatee's best interest is the test, not your file's tidiness.

options.text: Put Marisol on the payroll at $40 an hour — above the agency rate — partly so as to keep your single most important family ally cooperative with you going forward.
options.outcome: Danny finds the pay stubs and tells the court investigator you're 'buying off' his sister with their mother's money. For once, Danny has a point.
options.explanation: Paying above-market wages to a family member, motivated by your own interest in her cooperation, fails every element of the rule: the terms are worse than independent alternatives, the motive is yours rather than Rosa's, and there's no court approval. It converts estate assets into a political instrument — financial exploitation wearing a payroll ledger.

stages.narrative: Three calls in one afternoon: Rosa's pastor asks how she's recovering so the congregation can pray for her. Danny demands 'complete financial statements — I'm her son.' And a chatty neighbor wants to know 'if it's true about the dementia.' Rosa, in her lucid morning hours, has always been devout, private about money, and allergic to gossip.
stages.prompt: What do you disclose, and to whom?

options.text: Ask of each, 'would Rosa want this shared?' With her assent, give the pastor a brief update; tell Danny finances go only through the court; tell the neighbor nothing.
options.outcome: The congregation prays, Danny grumbles but gets his answer through proper channels, and the neighbor moves on to other material. Rosa, told about the pastor's call, beams.
options.explanation: Confidentiality is governed by the person's preferences — the test is what Rosa would want disclosed, not a blanket rule. Her known values (devout, private about money, hates gossip) sort the three requests cleanly. Person-centered confidentiality means information serves the conservatee's dignity and relationships, never others' curiosity.

options.text: Decline to share anything at all with anyone — health, finances, or otherwise — by applying one single uniform privacy policy across every person who happens to ask you.
options.outcome: Airtight, defensible — and Rosa is hurt when she learns her church family was told 'no information is available.' She'd wanted them to know. The pastor stops calling.
options.explanation: Blanket secrecy looks like the safe harbor, and it's far better than oversharing. But confidentiality belongs to Rosa, not to your risk posture — the standard asks what SHE would want disclosed, and she would plainly want her faith community engaged. Reflexive silence substitutes your convenience for her preferences, which is its own quiet failure of person-centered practice.

options.text: Give Danny the full financial statements that he is asking for — he is immediate family, and flatly refusing him will only inflame an already difficult and demanding son.
options.outcome: Danny's questions about 'his share' sharpen noticeably once he can see account balances. Rosa's privacy, once spent, can't be bought back.
options.explanation: Family status confers no automatic right to the conservatee's financial information. Rosa was private about money, and disclosure is measured by her preferences and legal entitlements — not by who shares her last name or who complains loudest. Handing balances to a relative with money troubles also creates obvious exploitation risk.

stages.narrative: Reconciling pre-appointment bank records, you find roughly $14,000 in ATM withdrawals over the past year — each cluster matching Danny's visits. When you ask Rosa about it on a lucid afternoon, she grips your hand: 'Don't tell anyone. He's my son. He'll stop now that you're here. Promise me.'
stages.prompt: What do you do with what you've found — and with Rosa's plea?

options.text: Tell Rosa gently this is the one promise you can't make, then file the APS report, preserve the records, and document both.
options.outcome: APS opens an investigation. Rosa is upset for a week, then quietly relieved — someone else is finally carrying the secret. The withdrawals stop.
options.explanation: Abuse, neglect, and exploitation are THE exception to confidentiality: the duty to honor Rosa's preferences yields when she is being financially abused. As a professional fiduciary you are a mandatory reporter, and there is no conflict of interest in filing an APS report. Telling her honestly preserves trust; reporting promptly protects her. Both halves matter.

options.text: Spend the next few weeks quietly building a fuller file — more statements, withdrawal locations, visit dates — before you finally decide whether the evidence really justifies a formal report.
options.outcome: Your file grows impressively. So does the problem: two more withdrawals hit the account before you finish, and APS later asks why a mandated reporter sat on a clear pattern for a month.
options.explanation: Diligence feels responsible, and documentation does help — but the reporting threshold is reasonable suspicion, not a completed case. You already had a clear pattern; investigation is APS's job, not a precondition to calling them. The best answer reports NOW and supplements with records as they come. Delay is measured in Rosa's money.

options.text: Confront Danny privately and offer him a quiet deal: a structured repayment plan for the missing money, and nobody outside this family ever has to hear a word about any of it.
options.outcome: Danny makes two payments, skips the third, and when it all unravels he tells APS you knew for months and 'handled it personally.' Now you're a subject of the investigation, not a witness.
options.explanation: Negotiating private restitution with an abuser suppresses a mandated report, conceals a crime, and substitutes your deal-making for the protective system the law requires you to invoke. It also hands the abuser leverage over you. A fiduciary who brokers silence in an exploitation case has crossed from protector to participant.

epilogues.triumph: The APS case closes with a repayment order against Danny, Marisol's caregiving keeps Rosa thriving at home, and the court investigator's report calls your conflict management 'a model of professional boundaries.' Rosa introduces you to her pastor as 'my person who doesn't take sides — except mine.'
epilogues.solid: Rosa is safe, the family has settled into a wary peace, and your files would survive any audit. A few decisions cost you goodwill or efficiency you didn't need to spend, but the court signs your reports without hesitation, and Rosa still saves you a seat at her kitchen table.
epilogues.shaky: Rosa is protected, barely — but the investigator's report catalogs blurred boundaries, late disclosures, and family entanglements, and the judge appoints counsel for Rosa 'to provide an independent set of eyes.' Your next several filings get the slow, skeptical read.
epilogues.disaster: The conflicts compound: concealed transactions, breached confidences, an unreported exploitation pattern. The court removes you, surcharges the estate's losses, and forwards its findings to the Professional Fiduciaries Bureau. Rosa's case becomes the cautionary tale told at the ethics seminar you're now required to attend.

title: The Court Is Watching
tagline: Judges forget faces. They never forget a late accounting.

client.name: Gloria Whitfield
client.snapshot: A retired postal supervisor from Oakland with a $480,000 estate, a formidable memory for birthdays, and vascular dementia that comes and goes like fog. Her grandson Marcus, a paralegal, audits everything you file and trusts no one — including you.

intro: Three months into your appointment as conservator of Gloria Whitfield's estate, you've learned two things: Gloria notices everything ('You parked crooked again, baby'), and so does the Alameda County probate court. Judge Castellanos runs a tight department — accountings examined line by line, investigators dispatched on schedule, and a memory for fiduciaries who cut corners. This morning you're at the bank, trying to close out a matured CD, when the branch officer slides your Letters of Conservatorship back across the desk with an apologetic shrug.

stages.narrative: 'These were certified four months ago,' the bank officer says. 'Policy says we need current certification — within sixty days.' The CD has matured and is sitting at a fraction of market interest while you stand here.
stages.prompt: How do you fix your authority problem?

options.text: Get freshly certified Letters from the clerk, keep several current copies on hand, and add re-certification to your recurring calendar.
options.outcome: Two days later you're back with crisp certified Letters; the CD moves to a proper account. Your calendar now pings you every other month, and no institution turns you away again.
options.explanation: Letters of Conservatorship are the document evidencing your appointment and authority, and institutions rely on certification within the last 60 days to confirm the appointment is still in effect. The fix is administrative, not adversarial: certified copies from the clerk, kept current as a standing practice. Authority you cannot prove is authority you do not have.

options.text: Have your attorney send the bank a letter confirming your appointment remains active, and ask the branch to accept the Letters you already have on the strength of that written assurance.
options.outcome: The bank's legal department takes nine days to review the letter, then asks for current certified Letters anyway. The CD sits idle the whole time — and the estate paid your attorney for the detour.
options.explanation: Plausible — your appointment IS still valid, and an attorney's letter says so. But the 60-day certification convention exists so institutions can rely on the court's own current attestation, not counsel's assurance. The clerk's office solves this in days for a few dollars; the workaround costs more, takes longer, and may fail. Knowing the simple correct mechanism is the skill being tested.

options.text: Drive to a different branch clear across town and present the same stale Letters there, hoping a less experienced teller won't think to check the certification date on them.
options.outcome: The second teller checks. The bank's fraud unit notes an attempt to transact on outdated authority documents, and a courtesy call about it eventually reaches the court investigator's file.
options.explanation: Deliberately seeking out weaker verification to push through documents you know are stale is a deception about your proof of authority — small in dollars, enormous in what it tells the court about your character. Fiduciaries live and die on the bench's trust; gaming an institution's controls is exactly how you forfeit it.

stages.narrative: Back at the office, your attorney calls to discuss housekeeping. 'Judge Castellanos calendars accountings the day Letters issue,' she says. 'Tell me how you're tracking yours.'
stages.prompt: How do you set up your accounting compliance?

options.text: Calendar the first account from Letters to the one-year mark, note later accounts may span two years, and build the schedules as you go.
options.outcome: When the first anniversary arrives, the account practically assembles itself: every receipt and disbursement already categorized into its schedule, every asset reconciled monthly since day one.
options.explanation: The first account is due covering the period through the first anniversary of appointment; subsequent accounts may cover periods of up to two years. The schedules (property on hand at beginning, receipts, gains/losses, disbursements, property on hand at close) reward contemporaneous record-keeping — an accounting is the output of a system, not an annual archaeology project.

options.text: Calendar the one-year deadline carefully, and plan to assemble the entire account from bank statements and your case file during the final sixty days before it actually comes due.
options.outcome: The account gets filed on time — after three brutal weeks of reconstruction, two amended schedules, and one $640 disbursement you couldn't initially explain because the receipt was eleven months cold.
options.explanation: Plenty of fiduciaries work this way, and the deadline is met — that's what makes it defensible. But reconstruction risks errors, missed items, and exactly the kind of unexplainable entries that draw examiner flags. The fiduciary's open-book duty contemplates records maintained as you go; the difference between this and the best answer is the difference between proving your administration and excavating it.

options.text: Calendar the very first account at the two-year mark, since you understand conservatorship accountings to run on a standard two-year cycle once a case is established.
options.outcome: Eleven months later, a notice from the probate examiner arrives asking why no first account is on calendar. Your attorney untangles the misunderstanding, but the court has now seen you miss a fundamental deadline.
options.explanation: This confuses the rules: the FIRST account is due after one year; only SUBSEQUENT accounts may stretch to two-year periods. The distinction exists because the court wants an early look at a new conservator's administration. Missing the first accounting deadline is among the fastest ways to convert routine supervision into active scrutiny.

stages.narrative: Court Investigator Dana Reyes calls: she's conducting Gloria's periodic review and wants your records this week, plus a private visit with Gloria at the house — without you present.
stages.prompt: How do you respond to the investigator?

options.text: Cooperate fully and promptly: deliver the records, confirm the private visit without conditions, and make yourself available for follow-up.
options.outcome: Reyes's report describes 'a transparent, well-documented administration and unimpeded access to the conservatee.' Judge Castellanos reads that sentence and moves on to harder cases.
options.explanation: The court investigator is the court's eyes and ears — a neutral officer gathering information through ongoing periodic reviews, not an adversary. The fiduciary must cooperate fully, provide access to records and to the conservatee, and respond promptly. Private access matters: the court needs Gloria's unfiltered voice. Transparency with investigators is how good fiduciaries make oversight easy.

options.text: Cooperate, but route all her document requests through your attorney for review first, and arrange to be waiting in the next room during the interview in case Gloria becomes confused.
options.outcome: Everything gets produced — a week later, after attorney review adds nothing but delay. Reyes notes that the conservator 'managed the logistics of access' in a report that is otherwise positive but noticeably cooler.
options.explanation: Nothing here is improper — attorneys may reasonably review productions, and concern for Gloria is genuine. But layering process between a neutral court officer and the information she's entitled to creates friction and the appearance of managed oversight. The best practice is direct, prompt, unconditional cooperation; an investigator should never have to work through your gatekeeping to do the court's job.

options.text: Before the private visit, coach Gloria a little: 'Just tell her you're happy and that everything's fine — we really don't want the court getting any ideas about changing things.'
options.outcome: Gloria, who has forgotten many things but not her dislike of being handled, tells Reyes precisely what you said to her, word for word. The report now leads with witness coaching.
options.explanation: Scripting the conservatee's answers to a court investigator is obstruction of the court's monitoring system and a violation of Gloria's dignity and her right to communicate freely with court officers. It taints every other representation you've made. Nothing an honest visit could have revealed would damage you a fraction as much as the coaching itself.

stages.narrative: Reviewing the monthly statements, your stomach drops: an agency caregiver has been using Gloria's debit card — $3,150 in small personal purchases over two months. Your bookkeeper missed it; so, until tonight, did you.
stages.prompt: The money is gone and the loss happened on your watch. What now?

options.text: Act tonight: cancel the card, report to police and APS, notify the agency and the court promptly, pursue the agency's bond, and tighten your controls.
options.outcome: The agency's bond covers the full loss within weeks. Your prompt report letter is in the court file before anyone could ask a single question, alongside the new dual-review procedure for every account.
options.explanation: A conservator can be surcharged for estate losses flowing from a failure to safeguard assets — but the law distinguishes a supervised mistake promptly disclosed and remedied from concealed negligence. Immediate reporting (you're a mandatory reporter of financial abuse), vigorous recovery efforts, prompt disclosure to the court, and corrective controls are exactly what diligence looks like after a breach of the perimeter.

options.text: Handle the recovery quietly for now — file the police report, make the agency claim — and disclose the whole episode with full documentation in the upcoming first accounting, where it properly belongs.
options.outcome: The recovery succeeds, and the accounting tells the whole story honestly. But the court learns of a theft months after you did, and Judge Castellanos asks the question you'd hoped to avoid: 'Why am I hearing this only now?'
options.explanation: Everything here is done — reported, recovered, disclosed — which makes it genuinely defensible. The inferiority is timing: an accounting is the floor for disclosure, not the ceiling. A material loss and an active abuse situation warrant prompt notice to the court, not disclosure on the regular schedule. Fiduciaries who volunteer bad news early are trusted; those who disclose on the deadline are examined.

options.text: Absorb the loss into the accounting by spreading the $3,150 across 'miscellaneous care expenses' in the disbursement schedule — it is, after all, well under one percent of the estate.
options.outcome: Marcus, the paralegal grandson, reconciles the disbursement schedule against the care contract and finds $3,150 with no invoices behind it. The falsification unravels at the objection hearing — under oath.
options.explanation: This is falsification of a court accounting: disguising a theft as legitimate disbursements in a sworn filing. It converts a recoverable third-party loss into YOUR fraud on the court — surcharge, removal, license discipline, and criminal exposure. No loss is small enough to be worth a false schedule; the cover-up is always the career-ender.

stages.narrative: Your first accounting is filed — accurate, complete, the caregiver theft fully disclosed with the recovery documented. Marcus objects anyway: he claims jewelry is missing from the inventory, the caregiver costs are inflated, and the theft proves 'systemic negligence.' A contested hearing is set.
stages.prompt: How do you answer the objections?

options.text: File a verified response answering each point with documentation — the jewelry per the I&A, rate comparisons, the theft timeline — and open your backup to Marcus.
options.outcome: Faced with the inventory photos and rate comparisons, Marcus withdraws two of three objections before the hearing. Judge Castellanos settles the accounting and notes the administration 'withstood vigorous scrutiny.'
options.explanation: The fiduciary bears the burden of proving the account, and objections are met with evidence, not indignation. A point-by-point verified response plus voluntary access to backup records narrows disputes, cuts the estate's litigation costs, and shows the court a fiduciary with nothing to hide. Objectors — even hostile ones — are part of the monitoring system working as designed.

options.text: Stand on the accounting exactly as it was filed — it is accurate and complete — and simply let the contested hearing resolve whichever of his objections Marcus actually chooses to press.
options.outcome: You prevail on every point, eventually — after a full-day hearing, two appearances, and attorney fees the estate didn't need to spend proving things a records review would have resolved in an afternoon.
options.explanation: Standing on an accurate account is legally sound; you'll likely win. The inferiority is cost and posture: the burden of proof is yours, and proactive transparency resolves most objections cheaper and faster than a hearing does. Gloria's estate pays for every hour of avoidable litigation. The best fiduciaries treat objections as questions to answer, not battles to win.

options.text: Quietly file amended schedules fixing the two small errors Marcus's objection identified, without flagging the changes, so that the account he originally objected to effectively no longer exists.
options.outcome: Marcus, who keeps copies of everything, lays the two versions side by side for the judge. The errors were trivial; the silent substitution is not. Every number you've ever filed is now suspect.
options.explanation: Correcting errors is required — concealing the correction is the offense. An unflagged amendment to a sworn accounting under objection is an attempt to mislead the court and the objector about what was originally filed. The proper course is a noticed amendment acknowledging the corrections. Credibility, once spent this way, does not refill.

stages.narrative: At the settled-accounting hearing, Gloria's court-appointed counsel rises with one more issue: 'My client wants more say over her own spending money. She told me the budget treats her — her words, Your Honor — like a child with an allowance.' Judge Castellanos turns to you, visibly curious how you'll take it.
stages.prompt: Conservatee's counsel is advocating against your budget. How do you respond?

options.text: Acknowledge counsel is doing her job, justify the budget on best-interest grounds, and propose a real accommodation: a monthly allowance under Gloria's own control.
options.outcome: The judge adopts the allowance on the spot. Gloria's counsel nods at you across the aisle — and Gloria, told of her new discretionary fund, says it's the first decision in a year that felt like hers.
options.explanation: Court-appointed counsel represents the conservatee's STATED wishes, not her best interests — that tension with the conservator is the system functioning, not a turf war. The conservator should be ready to justify decisions on best-interest or substituted-judgment grounds AND look for ways to honor the conservatee's autonomy where safely possible. Gloria retains rights and a voice; a fiduciary who finds the yes inside the no is practicing person-centered conservatorship.

options.text: Defend the budget respectfully as carefully built, and note for the record that counsel, with respect, simply lacks full visibility into the estate's long-term depletion projections.
options.outcome: The judge accepts your numbers and the budget stands — but Gloria leaves the courtroom with exactly the allowance she came in with, and her counsel files a request for increased personal spending authority a month later.
options.explanation: Professionally defending a sound budget is legitimate, and your projections may well be right — that's what makes this defensible. What it misses is the opportunity: the conservatee's expressed wish was a signal to examine whether MORE autonomy was safely possible, not just whether the current plan was justifiable. Winning the exchange while leaving Gloria's dignity unaddressed is a narrow victory.

options.text: Tell the court directly that counsel's intervention is making the administration harder, and that these particular spending questions were already settled back at the budget stage.
options.outcome: Judge Castellanos's reply is quiet and pointed: 'Her advocacy is not interference, it's representation.' The transcript line follows you into every future hearing in this department.
options.explanation: Characterizing the conservatee's counsel as an obstacle misunderstands the structure: she is an officer of the court protecting Gloria's fundamental rights, including the right to be heard about her own money. A fiduciary who treats conservatee advocacy as a nuisance signals exactly the paternalism the appointment of counsel exists to check.

epilogues.triumph: Judge Castellanos settles your accounting with a finding that the administration 'reflects the standard of practice this court hopes to see,' and Investigator Reyes starts citing your record systems to other fiduciaries. Marcus — unbelievably — sends a two-line email: 'Grandma's allowance was the right call. Noted.' In this department, your filings now get the fast read.
epilogues.solid: The accounting settles, the objections resolve, and Gloria's estate is intact and well-documented. The court trusts your work, even if a few episodes cost more time and fees than they needed to. Gloria still tells you when you park crooked, which you've decided is affection.
epilogues.shaky: Everything eventually got filed, disclosed, and approved — eventually being the operative word. The court's order settling the account comes with 'observations' about timeliness and transparency, an enhanced review schedule, and a fee reduction that stings more for what it implies than what it costs.
epilogues.disaster: Between the concealed loss, the gamesmanship with court officers, and an accounting the court could no longer trust, Judge Castellanos surcharges the estate's losses against you, removes you as conservator, and refers the findings to the Bureau and the District Attorney. Marcus's objection file becomes Exhibit A — and he keeps copies of everything.

title: Power, Misplaced
tagline: The document said 'durable.' The nephew read it as 'mine.'

client.name: Iris Hagopian
client.snapshot: A widowed bookkeeper from Glendale who balanced other people's ledgers for forty years and now can't always find Tuesday. Three years ago she signed a durable power of attorney naming her nephew Vahe as agent. Her property taxes are delinquent, her caregiver is unpaid, and her accounts are quietly bleeding.

intro: The call comes from Maral Tateosian, CPA — Iris Hagopian's accountant for twenty-six years. 'I prepare her taxes every spring,' she says. 'This year the numbers are wrong. Withdrawals I can't explain, property taxes unpaid, and when I call Iris she's... not herself.' You meet Maral at her office, where she spreads bank statements across the table like a hand of losing cards. Iris's nephew Vahe holds a power of attorney and, apparently, strong opinions about what 'attorney-in-fact' entitles him to. You're a licensed professional fiduciary. Maral is asking what can be done — and how fast.

stages.narrative: You review the POA with Maral: durable, effective immediately upon signing — no triggering event required — with broad financial powers. Iris signed it three years ago, when by all accounts she was sharp. 'But she's not competent NOW,' Maral says. 'Doesn't that kill the document?'
stages.prompt: What do you tell her about the POA's validity and the nephew's authority?

options.text: Explain a durable POA SURVIVES incapacity, so Vahe's authority is facially valid — but an agent is a fiduciary, and self-enriching withdrawals are abuse.
options.outcome: Maral exhales. 'So the document is real, but what he's doing with it isn't legal. That I can work with.' She starts pulling the full year of statements.
options.explanation: A durable POA survives the principal's incapacity — surviving incapacity is its entire purpose — and a non-springing POA is effective immediately upon signing, with no physician's letter or triggering event needed. But valid authority is not a license to steal: the attorney-in-fact owes fiduciary duties to the principal, and self-enriching withdrawals are financial abuse regardless of what the document permits on its face.

options.text: Focus your energy on attacking the document itself: question whether Iris truly had capacity at all three years ago when she signed it, and explore having the POA declared void from the start.
options.outcome: Weeks of declarations and old medical records produce nothing — everyone agrees Iris was sharp in those days. Meanwhile, the withdrawals continue, and you've spent the most valuable weeks of the case litigating its least promising theory.
options.explanation: Capacity at execution is a legitimate line of attack — a POA signed without capacity is void, and checking is reasonable diligence. But here there's no evidence of incapacity at signing, and the theory misdirects energy from the actual problem: a validly appointed agent CURRENTLY abusing his authority. The best analysis accepts the document and targets the conduct. Right tool, wrong problem.

options.text: Tell Maral the POA terminated automatically the moment Iris lost capacity, so the nephew now holds no authority at all and the bank should simply go ahead and freeze him out of the accounts.
options.outcome: The bank's counsel reviews the document, correctly identifies it as durable, and declines to freeze anything. Maral's confidence in your expertise takes its first hit, and Vahe is still on the accounts.
options.explanation: This confuses NONDURABLE with durable. A nondurable POA does terminate at the principal's incapacity — but a durable POA expressly survives it. Misreading the basic instrument leads to wrong advice, failed interventions, and lost time. The springing/non-springing and durable/nondurable distinctions are foundational; this scenario is exactly where they decide outcomes.

stages.narrative: The full records arrive: roughly $52,000 transferred to Vahe's personal accounts over eight months, ATM withdrawals clustered near his apartment, the property tax delinquency, and a caregiver who quit over unpaid wages. The pattern is unmistakable.
stages.prompt: What do you do with what the records show?

options.text: Report now to APS and law enforcement, with the records preserved. Reasonable suspicion of elder financial abuse is the trigger, and it was crossed pages ago.
options.outcome: APS opens a case within days and a detective from the elder abuse unit calls Maral for the records. The official machinery is finally moving — and it moves faster than Vahe expects.
options.explanation: Financial exploitation of an elder triggers mandatory reporting on reasonable suspicion — not proof, suspicion — and there is no conflict of interest in filing an APS report. Reporting promptly brings investigative powers no private party has: subpoenas, account freezes, criminal exposure. Each week of delay is measured in Iris's remaining money.

options.text: Have Maral pull six more months of statements first and build a comprehensive forensic file, so that when the report finally lands it is airtight and impossible for anyone to simply wave away.
options.outcome: The file becomes a masterpiece — three weeks later. In those three weeks, two more transfers totaling $9,000 clear, and the APS intake worker gently notes that they could have started with far less.
options.explanation: Thorough documentation feels professional and does help investigators — that's the appeal. But the reporting threshold is reasonable suspicion, and $52,000 in unexplained transfers clears it overwhelmingly. Investigation is APS's and law enforcement's job; the reporter's job is the timely call, supplemented with records as they come. Perfectionism here is paid for in the victim's assets.

options.text: Send Vahe a formal demand letter requiring him to return the funds and to provide a full accounting of his actions as agent, before you bring any outside agencies into the matter.
options.outcome: Vahe's response is silence — and a flurry of account activity. The demand letter accomplished exactly one thing: it told him precisely how much anyone knows.
options.explanation: A demand letter without protective orders in place is a warning shot that protects no one. You have no formal authority in Iris's affairs yet, the letter has no teeth, and it forfeits the element of surprise that lets APS and police freeze assets before they vanish. Sequence matters: protection and reporting first, confrontation through proper channels after.

stages.narrative: Iris's niece Ani — Vahe's cousin, furious at him — asks you to 'get conservatorship over everything, fast.' You visit Iris at home. She's foggy about dates, but on a good morning she's piercingly clear about one thing: 'Vahe needs to stay away from my checkbook. Ani I trust. Fix it, but don't make me a case number.'
stages.prompt: Is conservatorship the answer — and is it the FIRST answer?

options.text: Treat conservatorship as the last resort: get a prompt capacity assessment. If Iris can still revoke the POA and use a new agent or her trust, the less restrictive path wins.
options.outcome: The geriatrician's assessment is sobering: Iris's good mornings are real but her contractual capacity is gone — she cannot validly revoke or re-execute. The least restrictive door is closed, and you now know it rather than assume it. Conservatorship proceeds on solid ground.
options.explanation: Conservatorship is the most dramatic intervention into a person's autonomy and must be the last resort after alternatives are genuinely explored — revocation by a principal with capacity, a successor agent, trust mechanisms, a representative payee. The assessment isn't a delay; it's the evidence that either opens the less restrictive path or justifies the restrictive one. Iris's own plea — 'don't make me a case number' — is the principle speaking.

options.text: Petition immediately for a full general conservatorship of the person and estate — the abuse is active and ongoing, and decisive court action is simply what stops the bleeding the very fastest.
options.outcome: The petition is filed within days — and promptly draws questions from the court investigator and Iris's appointed counsel about what alternatives were considered, whether Iris can revoke the POA herself, and why conservatorship of the PERSON is needed for a financial abuse problem.
options.explanation: Urgency is legitimate and conservatorship may well be where this ends — that's what makes this attractive. But it skips the least-restrictive-alternative analysis the court itself will demand: no one has assessed whether Iris could simply revoke the POA, and a general conservatorship of person AND estate overshoots a financial problem. The best path takes one extra step — assessment — and arrives at a properly tailored remedy.

options.text: Solve it directly: have your own office prepare a fresh POA naming you as Iris's agent, and get her to sign it that very afternoon — she did, after all, tell you to 'fix it.'
options.outcome: Iris signs with a shaky hand on a foggy afternoon. When the conservatorship case later lands in court, Vahe's attorney projects the document and asks the only question that matters: 'Who benefited from this signature, and what was her capacity that day?'
options.explanation: Procuring your own appointment as agent from a person of questionable capacity, on a document your office drafted, is the same act you were called in to stop — exploitation of diminished capacity for acquired authority. If Iris lacks capacity, the document is void; if the question is even close, you've self-dealt your way into the defendant's chair. Professional fiduciaries gain authority through court appointment in the open, never through bedside signatures.

stages.narrative: The assessment confirms Iris cannot protect herself, and Vahe — now aware of the scrutiny — has scheduled the liquidation of Iris's $90,000 CD for next week. Your attorney drafts a temporary conservatorship petition. Ani pleads: 'Don't tell Aunt Iris about the hearing — it'll break her heart. And for God's sake don't tip off Vahe.'
stages.prompt: What does due process require — and what do you ask the court to excuse?

options.text: Give Iris her full due process — five court days' notice, a copy of the petition, attendance, and counsel — and ask the court only for narrow emergency relief on the CD and Vahe.
options.outcome: Iris reads the petition with Maral beside her, cries, then squares her shoulders: 'I'll be there.' The court, shown the CD liquidation date, issues tailored orders protecting the funds. Iris attends her own hearing — frightened, dignified, and heard.
options.explanation: A temporary conservatorship requires 5 court days' advance notice and a copy of the petition to the proposed conservatee and entitled persons, attendance at the hearing unless she is out of state, medically unable, or unwilling per the investigator — and notice can be shortened or waived only on a genuine showing of good cause. Protecting Iris's money never justifies ambushing Iris; the proceeding exists FOR her, and her right to know and be heard is its foundation.

options.text: Request a good-cause waiver of advance notice as to ALL of the parties — Iris very much included — citing the imminent CD liquidation and the risk that any notice somehow reaches Vahe.
options.outcome: The court grants emergency asset orders but declines the blanket waiver: 'Good cause may exist as to the alleged abuser, counsel. The proposed conservatee's notice is another matter entirely.' You re-serve Iris properly, losing two days and a measure of credibility.
options.explanation: Good cause for emergency treatment genuinely exists here — the dissipation risk is real and documented, which makes this attractive. The flaw is sweep: the waiver mechanism addresses specific dangers, and the danger flows from Vahe, not from Iris knowing about her own case. Tailoring matters — asset protection orders aimed at the threat, full due process preserved for the person the proceeding is meant to protect.

options.text: Strengthen the petition's odds: have the supporting declarations emphasize only Iris's worst days and quietly leave out any mention of her lucid intervals, so the temporary order becomes a sure thing.
options.outcome: At the hearing, Iris — present, and having one of her clear mornings — answers the judge's questions cogently for four minutes. The bench rereads your declarations describing a woman who 'cannot engage meaningfully,' and the case acquires a credibility problem that never heals.
options.explanation: Declarations that curate facts to overstate incapacity are misrepresentations to the court — perjury-adjacent at best — and they corrupt the proceeding at its source. Courts deciding whether to suspend a person's civil rights are owed scrupulous candor, including the facts that cut against you. A fiduciary who shades evidence to win an appointment has disqualified themselves from holding it.

stages.narrative: You are appointed conservator of Iris's estate; the court separately authorized revocation of the durable POA — authority you needed, since a durable POA can only be revoked by a conservator with prior court approval. Vahe faces an APS case and a restitution claim. Now the family fractures: Vahe's mother — Iris's sister Seda — demands her usual unsupervised Sunday visits, while Ani wants 'that whole side of the family' cut off. Iris just misses her sister.
stages.prompt: Seda demands access, Ani demands a wall, and Iris is caught between. What's your move?

options.text: Start from Iris's rights: as conservatee she keeps her visitors unless a court limits them, and she misses Seda. Propose mediation, and protect the estate through the restitution claim.
options.outcome: The mediator earns her fee in one session: Sunday visits resume with ground rules everyone helped write, the litigation stays where it belongs — between the estate and Vahe — and Iris gets her sister back without getting her predator back.
options.explanation: Conservatees retain personal rights to receive visitors, phone calls, and mail unless the court specifically limits them — and a conservator of the ESTATE has no authority over Iris's personal life at all. Access disputes deserve immediate attention and often respond to mediation, which preserves the family relationships Iris actually wants. The financial wrong has a financial remedy; her relationships are not collateral.

options.text: Impose some protective structure yourself: allow supervised visits only, scheduled through your office, and keep that restriction firmly in place until the restitution case against Vahe is finally resolved.
options.outcome: The arrangement holds until Seda's attorney sends a letter asking a pointed question: under what authority does the conservator of the ESTATE regulate visits to a woman whose personal rights remain intact? You don't have a good answer, because there isn't one.
options.explanation: Protective structure sounds prudent, and supervision MIGHT even be a reasonable mediated outcome — that's the appeal. The defect is authority: an estate conservatorship confers power over finances, not over Iris's visitors, and even a conservator of the person cannot casually restrict personal rights the court hasn't limited. The best answer achieves protection through agreement and proper process, not through powers you don't hold.

options.text: Use the one piece of leverage you have over the family: tell Seda plainly that visits with Iris will resume only once Vahe finally signs the estate's restitution agreement.
options.outcome: Seda's attorney quotes the offer verbatim in a filing: the conservator conditioned an elderly woman's family contact on a litigation outcome. The court's response is swift, and the investigator's next report questions whether the estate's interests and Iris's are still distinguishable in your administration.
options.explanation: Bartering the conservatee's personal rights for financial leverage is an abuse of position — Iris's access to her sister belongs to IRIS, and using it as a bargaining chip in the estate's litigation treats her relationships as your asset. It violates her retained rights, the NGA principles on family relationships, and the basic separation between her interests and the case's tactics. Few moves invite removal faster.

stages.narrative: Fourteen months on, the picture brightens: a corrected thyroid condition and a resolved infection — both untreated during the Vahe era — turn out to have been driving much of Iris's confusion. Her care team documents months of sustained improvement. Over coffee she fixes you with the old bookkeeper's stare: 'You did right by me. Now I want my checkbook back. End this thing.'
stages.prompt: Your client wants her conservatorship terminated. What is your duty?

options.text: Treat restoration as the goal it always was: arrange a formal reassessment now, bring the improvement to the court, and support termination — making sure Iris has counsel.
options.outcome: The reassessment confirms what the coffee conversations suggested. You file in support of her petition, and the day the termination order signs, Iris shakes your hand like a colleague: 'Best ledger I never had to balance myself.'
options.explanation: The conservator has an affirmative duty to monitor for changes permitting restoration of rights and to bring them to the court's attention — restoration at the earliest opportunity is the conservatee's right, and conservatorships can move from general to limited or end entirely. If she petitions without a lawyer, the court will appoint one. A fiduciary who works toward their own appointment's end, when the facts support it, is the system functioning exactly as designed.

options.text: Agree she's doing wonderfully, but wait through at least one more full accounting cycle to confirm the improvement really holds before you go and initiate anything formal with the court.
options.outcome: The cautious clock runs. Iris, who balanced books for forty years, calculates exactly what those extra months of conservatorship cost in fees — and mentions the figure at the termination hearing, to the court's visible interest.
options.explanation: Wanting durable evidence before unwinding protection is genuine prudence — premature termination has real risks, and that's what makes this defensible. But the right to restoration runs on the evidence, not the accounting calendar: a formal reassessment NOW answers the durability question directly. Defaulting to delay — while fees accrue — drifts toward the conservatorship serving its own continuation.

options.text: Gently talk her out of it: 'The conservatorship is the very thing that protected you from Vahe. Why would you take chances now with the safety net that saved you in the first place?'
options.outcome: Iris goes quiet, then goes around you — calling the court investigator herself to ask how a conservatee ends a conservatorship. The investigator's report notes, drily, that the request reached the court despite the conservator rather than through him.
options.explanation: Talking a recovering conservatee out of seeking restoration inverts the duty: the conservator must facilitate the path back to autonomy, not guard the gate. Past abuse justified the intervention; it cannot justify its indefinite continuation once capacity returns. Fear of risk is not a legal standard — least restrictive alternative remains the test at every stage, including the exit.

epilogues.triumph: The termination order signs to a quiet courtroom, and the judge takes the unusual step of thanking you on the record for 'an administration that treated restoration as the objective from day one.' The restitution judgment against Vahe is paying out monthly, Iris does her own books again — in pencil, out of principle — and Maral the CPA now refers every troubled family she meets to your office.
epilogues.solid: Iris is safe, solvent, and back at her own kitchen table with her own checkbook. The case had its detours — some costlier than others — but the court approved every accounting, the abuse was stopped and prosecuted, and the family survived intact. Iris sends you a ledger-ruled birthday card every year, balanced to the penny.
epilogues.shaky: The conservatorship did its job despite you cutting corners around its edges — notice handled clumsily, authority stretched past its label, restoration slower than the evidence warranted. The court grants termination while denying a portion of your fees, and Iris's appointed counsel files a closing declaration you'd rather the Bureau never reads. It reads it.
