epilogues.disaster: What began as a rescue ends as a removal: misleading declarations, rights traded as leverage, and a conservator arguing to keep a recovered woman under his authority. The court terminates the conservatorship, surcharges your fees, and refers the record to the Professional Fiduciaries Bureau and the District Attorney — whose elder abuse unit now has two files from this family, and your name is on the second one.

title: The Man in the Blue Sedan
tagline: A sister begs you to save her brother — but the law says you can't even file the petition.

client.name: Marcus Webb
client.snapshot: Marcus is a former electrician with schizophrenia and a severe alcohol use disorder, living out of his blue sedan in a Bakersfield parking lot. He is insulin-dependent but hasn't filled a prescription in four months. His sister Denise has been leaving food on his windshield because he won't open the door for anyone.

intro: Denise Webb sits across from you in your office, a folder of hospital discharge papers trembling in her hands. Her brother Marcus has been hospitalized on 72-hour holds three times this year, and each time he's released back to his car. She found your name on the Professional Fiduciaries Bureau website and wants to hire you today — to 'get an LPS conservatorship' over Marcus before his diabetes kills him. You can see she's done her homework, but not quite enough of it.

stages.narrative: Denise slides a retainer check across your desk. 'I read that LPS conservatorship is for people like Marcus — mentally ill, can't care for themselves. I want you to file the petition this week. Money is no object.'
stages.prompt: How do you respond to Denise's request that you petition for an LPS conservatorship over Marcus?

options.text: Explain that only the county may petition for an LPS conservatorship, help Denise make a referral, and discuss CARE Court.
options.outcome: Denise is deflated but grateful for the straight answer. Together you draft a detailed referral to the county documenting Marcus's hospitalizations, untreated diabetes, and substance use.
options.explanation: Under the Lanterman-Petris-Short Act, a private party — including a professional fiduciary — cannot initiate an LPS conservatorship. Only the county (acting through its designated officer, usually the Public Guardian) may petition, typically on referral from a treating facility. The professional answer is to redirect Denise to the proper channel, support the referral with documentation, and educate her on upstream alternatives. Knowing the limits of your own authority is itself a core fiduciary competency.

options.text: Suggest Denise instead petition for a general probate conservatorship of the person, which family members are allowed to initiate, so someone gains legal authority over Marcus quickly.
options.outcome: Denise files a probate petition, but Marcus's court-appointed counsel opposes it, arguing his needs stem from untreated mental illness — exactly what the LPS framework, not probate, was built for.
options.explanation: This is genuinely plausible — family members can petition for probate conservatorship, and a probate conservatorship of the estate is often more efficient for managing finances. But it is inferior here because a probate conservatorship cannot authorize the involuntary psychiatric treatment Marcus's grave disability requires. The LPS Act exists precisely for serious mental illness and severe substance use disorder; the best answer routes the case into the correct legal framework rather than the merely available one.

options.text: Accept the retainer and agree to draft and file an LPS petition for Denise, figuring the court will sort out any standing problems.
options.outcome: The court rejects the petition outright for lack of standing. Denise is out the filing costs, weeks have passed, and Marcus's condition has worsened.
options.explanation: Filing a petition you know (or should know) is legally impossible wastes the client's money and the critical window for intervention. A fiduciary who takes fees for work outside the bounds of the law violates the duty to act with prudence, care, and judgment under the Professional Fiduciaries Act.

stages.narrative: The county takes the referral. Two weeks later, Marcus is hospitalized again after a hypoglycemic collapse. The county's LPS investigator calls you: 'The family says you've been tracking this. He buys gas-station food and sleeps in his car — under the old standard, that's food and shelter. Tell me what you've got.'
stages.prompt: What input do you provide to the county investigator evaluating whether Marcus is gravely disabled?

options.text: Provide dated facts that Marcus can't provide for his own medical care or safety, and note SB 43 made both grave-disability criteria.
options.outcome: The investigator incorporates your documentation. The county's petition cites Marcus's inability to provide for necessary medical care and personal safety — squarely within the expanded statutory definition.
options.explanation: SB 43 (effective 1/1/2024, with all counties implementing by 1/1/2026) expanded 'gravely disabled' in two ways: it added severe substance use disorder (alone or co-occurring with mental illness) as a qualifying condition, and it expanded the criteria beyond food, clothing, and shelter to include inability to provide for personal safety and necessary medical care. Marcus's untreated diabetes is the textbook case the expansion was written for. Precise, documented facts tied to the current standard are the most useful thing a fiduciary can contribute.

options.text: Tell the investigator Marcus clearly needs help and that you'll defer completely to the clinical evaluators on whether he meets the legal grave-disability standard.
options.outcome: The clinicians reach the right conclusion eventually, but the petition is delayed while the county reconstructs the medical-noncompliance history you already had documented.
options.explanation: Deference to clinical judgment is appropriate humility — the fiduciary doesn't diagnose. But it is inferior because the grave-disability determination turns on concrete functional facts, and you possess documented evidence (missed prescriptions, collapse incidents) that directly maps onto the SB 43 criteria. The best practice is to supply documented observations while leaving the clinical and legal conclusions to the proper parties.

options.text: Tell the investigator that because Marcus feeds himself and his car gives him shelter, he probably doesn't meet the gravely disabled standard.
options.outcome: Your statement gives the county pause and nearly derails the petition — until the hospital's evaluator points out you were applying a definition that was superseded in 2024.
options.explanation: This answer applies the pre-SB 43 standard. The current definition asks whether the person can provide for food OR clothing OR shelter OR personal safety OR necessary medical care. A person can be marginally fed and sheltered and still be gravely disabled because they cannot manage life-sustaining medical treatment. Outdated legal knowledge produces wrong outcomes for real people.

stages.narrative: The hospital stabilizes Marcus and — to everyone's frustration — the county declines to proceed with LPS for now, finding him improved at discharge. Denise calls you in tears: 'So we just wait for him to almost die again?'
stages.prompt: What do you recommend as the next intervention for Marcus?

options.text: Help Denise petition CARE Court: his diagnosis makes him eligible, family may petition, and the court can order treatment and housing.
options.outcome: The CARE Court petition is accepted. Marcus, with appointed counsel and a supporter, grudgingly engages with a CARE plan that includes housing placement and medication support.
options.explanation: The CARE Act (SB 1338) created a civil process available statewide as an upstream alternative to LPS conservatorship. Unlike LPS, family members CAN petition. Eligibility fits Marcus: 18+, schizophrenia spectrum diagnosis. The court can order a CARE plan of up to 12 months, renewable once. This honors the least restrictive alternative principle — conservatorship is the last resort, and the law now provides a meaningful intermediate step. Notably, non-compliance with a CARE plan may be considered in any later LPS proceeding, so nothing is lost by trying it.

options.text: Advise Denise to keep detailed records and renew the LPS referral at the next crisis, when the evidence of grave disability will be undeniable.
options.outcome: Denise documents diligently. But the next crisis is a near-fatal one, and the family later asks why nobody mentioned there was a court process they could have started months earlier.
options.explanation: Documentation and renewed referral is sound, defensible practice — counties often need a fuller record. But it is inferior because it is purely reactive: it waits for deterioration when the CARE Act exists specifically to intervene before a person's condition substantially deteriorates to the point of conservatorship. The least restrictive alternative principle requires exploring available interventions, not just queuing up for the most restrictive one.

options.text: Tell Denise to re-file the same LPS referral with the county every few weeks until the office finally relents and agrees to petition for Marcus.
options.outcome: The county flags the file as a repeat referral with no new facts. Relations with the Public Guardian's office sour, which costs you credibility on future cases.
options.explanation: Repetition without new evidence changes nothing — the county's decision turns on whether the statutory standard is met at the time of evaluation. This approach burns professional relationships and ignores the actual gap: Marcus needs an engagement mechanism now, which CARE Court provides and repeated referrals do not.

stages.narrative: Eight months later, the picture has changed: a second LPS referral succeeded, the Public Guardian serves as LPS conservator of Marcus's person, and the probate court appointed you conservator of his estate to manage a $190,000 inheritance from his mother. At your first meeting, Marcus leans across the table: 'You're working with them. You're skimming my money. Prove you're not — give me $500 cash right now.'
stages.prompt: How do you handle Marcus's accusations and his demand for cash?

options.text: Stay calm, show him the statements, set a spending allowance with his input, and schedule regular visits so he can check the books.
options.outcome: Marcus scoffs, but he pockets the statement you printed for him. At the third visit, he asks a real question about his mother's house. The testing slowly tapers off.
options.explanation: Clients with serious mental illness may test the fiduciary's authority or experience paranoia that the fiduciary is tricking them — this is a known dynamic, not a personal attack. The professional response is consistency, transparency, and an 'open book': involve him in decisions to the greatest extent possible (NGA principle), document everything, and let predictable behavior do what argument cannot. You meet the demand's legitimate core — his right to know about his own money — without surrendering judgment to it.

options.text: Route the future financial conversations through Denise, whom Marcus trusts more, so the subject of money doesn't keep triggering his paranoia.
options.outcome: Things are quieter — until Marcus learns you've been talking to his sister about his money and becomes convinced the two of you are conspiring. The paranoia now has a plausible storyline.
options.explanation: Using a trusted family intermediary is a defensible de-escalation instinct, and family engagement has its place. But it is inferior because it excludes Marcus from decisions about his own life, contrary to the NGA principle of involving the person to the greatest extent possible — and Marcus, not Denise, is your client. Routing information around a paranoid client tends to confirm the paranoia rather than soothe it.

options.text: Stop the in-person visits and communicate only by certified letter, keeping a clean paper record and avoiding the confrontations his accusations provoke.
options.outcome: Marcus's court-appointed counsel reports to the court that the estate conservator hasn't seen the conservatee in months. The judge asks pointed questions at your next accounting.
options.explanation: Retreating to paper protects you, not him. The fiduciary's roles include monitor and liaison — you cannot assess his changing needs, spot exploitation, or maintain a working relationship through certified mail. Documentation should support the relationship, not replace it.

stages.narrative: Denise asks for a meeting. She's confused: 'The county says Marcus's conservatorship expires next year and they have to redo it. Yours doesn't. And neither of you will just make him take his medication. Can't you take over the whole thing and handle his psychiatric care too?'
stages.prompt: How do you explain the relationship between the LPS conservatorship and your probate estate appointment?

options.text: Explain the split: LPS runs one year, only the county renews it and it alone carries treatment authority, while your probate role covers only the estate.
options.outcome: Denise finally has a map of the system. She stops asking you to do the county's job and starts attending the LPS renewal hearings prepared.
options.explanation: LPS and probate conservatorships are governed by separate legal frameworks. LPS conservatorships automatically terminate after one year unless the county re-establishes them; they exist for grave disability and carry treatment authority a probate conservator never has. A probate conservatorship of the estate handles finances and is often the more efficient vehicle for that purpose. Knowing — and communicating — which authority lives where is fundamental to working a dual-track case, and consulting a lawyer on LPS/probate differences is expressly recommended practice.

options.text: Offer to petition the probate court to expand your appointment to conservator of the person too, so one professional oversees everything except the psychiatric hold authority.
options.outcome: The court declines, noting the LPS conservator of the person already holds personal-care authority and a parallel probate appointment would create overlapping, conflicting roles.
options.explanation: Consolidation under one fiduciary sounds efficient and shows initiative — but it misunderstands the structure. The Public Guardian, as LPS conservator, already holds authority over Marcus's person, including placement and treatment; a duplicate probate conservatorship of the person would add cost and confusion without adding the involuntary-treatment authority Denise actually wants, which no probate appointment can confer. The best answer educates rather than litigates.

options.text: Reassure Denise that once an LPS conservatorship is in place it simply continues until someone petitions to end it, so the family needn't worry about yearly renewals.
options.outcome: Nobody prepares for the renewal hearing. The conservatorship lapses when the county's evidence is thin, and Marcus disengages from treatment within weeks.
options.explanation: This is simply wrong on the law: LPS conservatorships terminate automatically after one year unless the county affirmatively re-establishes them — a deliberate due-process safeguard given the liberty interests at stake. A fiduciary who misstates the framework leaves the family unprepared for the system's most predictable event.

stages.narrative: Eighteen months in, the system has worked better than anyone hoped. Marcus is stable on a long-acting injectable, sober four months, living in a board-and-care, and working two shifts a week at a bike repair shop. He asks you, almost shyly: 'I want my paycheck in my own hands. And maybe... I don't need all this anymore.'
stages.prompt: How do you respond to Marcus's request for more financial control and his question about ending the conservatorship?

options.text: Tell him the law is on his side — a conservatee may control his own wages — then document his progress and support him raising restoration.
options.outcome: Marcus cashes his own paycheck for the first time in two years. At the next review, the court investigator's report describes a conservatorship moving deliberately toward restoration.
options.explanation: Conservatees retain the right to receive and control their own salary — this is an enumerated right, not a privilege you grant. More broadly, the guardian has an affirmative duty to monitor for changes that allow restoration of rights and to bring them to the court's attention; the right to restoration at the earliest opportunity belongs to Marcus. Conservatorship is a spectrum — plenary to limited to none — and the fiduciary's job includes working himself out of it when the facts support it.

options.text: Congratulate him, agree to raise his monthly allowance from the estate, and tell him you'll revisit the larger restoration questions at the next accounting.
options.outcome: Marcus accepts the larger allowance but notices his paycheck still routes through you. 'Even my own wages?' he asks. You don't have a good answer.
options.explanation: A measured increase in autonomy with review at the next milestone is cautious, defensible fiduciary practice. But it is inferior on two counts: it treats his statutory right to control his own wages as a discretionary allowance, and it defers the restoration duty to an administrative calendar. The duty to support restoration runs on the conservatee's progress, not the accounting cycle.

options.text: Decline for now, explaining that four months of sobriety is still fragile and that loosening the controls this early could set him up for a relapse.
options.outcome: Marcus's motivation visibly dims. His counsel raises the wage issue at the next hearing, and the court orders the change you refused — with commentary about your reasoning.
options.explanation: Protectiveness is not a substitute for legal accuracy: the wage right is his regardless of your relapse worries, and a blanket refusal disregards both the least restrictive alternative principle and his right to restoration at the earliest opportunity. Risk can be managed through supports and monitoring without denying retained rights.

epilogues.triumph: At the final review hearing, the judge notes that Marcus's case file reads like a textbook: the right doors knocked on in the right order, authority never exceeded, and a conservatee walking out with his rights restored and a fiduciary he — almost — trusts. The Public Guardian's office starts referring you their probate estate appointments.
epilogues.solid: Marcus is stable and the estate is intact, though the road had detours that better navigation would have avoided. The court approves your accountings without comment, and Denise sends a card that says, simply, 'Thank you for telling us the truth about the system.'
epilogues.shaky: The conservatorship survived, but the court's questions at your accounting were sharp: missed frameworks, delayed referrals, a conservatee kept at arm's length. The judge approves your fees — reduced — and suggests continuing education on the LPS Act and the CARE Act.
epilogues.disaster: Between the standing fiasco, the boundary violations, and the things that never made it into your reports, the court removes you as conservator of the estate and refers the file to the Professional Fiduciaries Bureau. Marcus's new fiduciary inherits a client more paranoid than ever — and this time, with reason.

title: What Eleanor Wanted
tagline: Everyone at the hospital has an opinion about how she should die. Your job is to find out what she actually said.

client.name: Eleanor Asante
client.snapshot: Eleanor is a retired choir director and the widow of a Pentecostal pastor, with advanced congestive heart failure and moderate dementia. Her faith is the architecture of her life. Her two children — Samuel, a deacon, and Ruth, an ICU nurse in Atlanta — disagree about nearly everything, including what their mother would want.

intro: You are appointed conservator of the person for Eleanor Asante after a contested hearing in which her children fought each other to a standstill. Your Letters are three days old when Mercy General calls: Eleanor has been admitted with fluid overload, and the hospitalist wants 'whoever makes her decisions' at a care conference tomorrow morning. In the hallway outside her room, Samuel tells you his mother believes healing comes through prayer; Ruth tells you her mother is drowning in her own chest. Eleanor, propped up on pillows, hums a hymn and asks if you've come to take her home.

stages.narrative: At the care conference, the hospitalist slides a consent packet toward you. 'You're the conservator — you sign now, right?' Samuel interjects that his mother did paperwork with her church attorney years ago, though no one has seen it.
stages.prompt: Before making any medical decisions, what is your first move?

options.text: Pause the consent and search for Eleanor's advance directive — the church attorney, her prior doctors, the recorder — before acting.
options.outcome: The church attorney produces an advance directive from nine years ago: a living will with detailed end-of-life instructions, naming her late husband as agent with no successor. The instructions now anchor every decision that follows.
options.explanation: The guardian has an affirmative duty to find any living will or advance directive — these documents are the most reliable evidence of the person's own wishes and they control the scope of surrogate authority. An existing DPAHC executed while Eleanor had capacity cannot simply be ignored or revoked by a conservator without prior court authority. Locating the documents before signing anything is the foundational act of surrogate medical decision-making; copies then go to her doctors and the facility.

options.text: Rely on your Letters of conservatorship to handle today's admission consents, and plan to track down any advance directive once the immediate decisions are behind you.
options.outcome: You sign the admission consents. Two weeks later the directive surfaces — and you learn one decision you made contradicts her written instructions, which you must now unwind.
options.explanation: Acting on your Letters is plausible — you are the appointed surrogate, and hospitals need decisions. But it is inferior because the directive, not your appointment, is the controlling evidence of Eleanor's wishes, and without exclusive medical authority your power coexists with hers and with any prior agent's. The few hours it takes to ask 'does a directive exist?' before consenting is the difference between substituted judgment and guessing.

options.text: Conclude that since neither child has actually seen the paperwork, no valid directive exists, and proceed at the conference as Eleanor's sole decision-maker.
options.outcome: The directive existed — recorded with her estate plan all along. Eleanor's court-appointed counsel asks the obvious question: did you look?
options.explanation: Absence of family knowledge is not absence of a document. The duty to search is the conservator's, and it means actually searching: attorneys, physicians, hospital records, the home. Skipping the search converts a knowable answer about Eleanor's wishes into your own assumptions — the precise failure surrogate decision-making law is designed to prevent.

stages.narrative: Eleanor's cardiologist recommends a procedure to place a pacemaker-defibrillator. Eleanor has good mornings and foggy afternoons. This morning she is bright, asking the nurses about their children by name.
stages.prompt: How do you handle consent for the recommended procedure?

options.text: Hold the consent talk on a good morning — risks, benefits, alternatives explained plainly — gauge her understanding, and document it.
options.outcome: Eleanor listens, asks whether the device would stop her from 'going when the Lord calls,' and says yes to the pacemaker but wants to talk more about the defibrillator. The cardiologist, impressed, adjusts the plan.
options.explanation: Informed consent means agreement with knowledge of risks, benefits, and alternatives — and a conservatee retains the right to receive information about treatment and to participate to the greatest extent possible. With fluctuating capacity, the standard practice is to engage the person at their best, explain to the extent they can understand, and document their responses and comprehension. Her question about the defibrillator is exactly the kind of values information that makes substituted judgment possible later.

options.text: Review the procedure carefully with Ruth, the ICU nurse, reach agreement with both children, and then sign the consent yourself on Eleanor's behalf.
options.outcome: The consent is signed and the medicine is sound — but Eleanor wakes from the procedure asking what the lump in her chest is. No one had told her.
options.explanation: Consulting the medically sophisticated family and building consensus is responsible practice, and the conservator may consent when the conservatee cannot. But it is inferior because it skips the person herself: Eleanor has lucid mornings and a retained right to be informed and involved. The NGA principles and the Handbook both require involving the person in decisions to the greatest extent possible — family agreement is a supplement to that, never a substitute.

options.text: Sign the consent right away — Eleanor carries a dementia diagnosis, so her input on the procedure is no longer legally meaningful anyway.
options.outcome: The procedure goes forward, but Eleanor's counsel later challenges your pattern of treating the diagnosis as a blanket incapacity finding.
options.explanation: A dementia diagnosis is not the same as a global lack of decisional capacity. Capacity is decision-specific and can fluctuate; a person may retain medical decision-making capacity on a good morning even with significant impairment. Equating diagnosis with incapacity erases retained rights and violates the duty to assess rather than presume.

stages.narrative: Back at her care home, Eleanor begins refusing her diuretics. 'Pastor Obeng is praying over me Tuesday,' she tells the med tech, serene. 'The Lord doesn't need water pills.' Her ankles are swelling. Samuel backs his mother completely; Ruth is on the phone within the hour, furious.
stages.prompt: How do you respond to Eleanor's faith-based refusal of her heart medication?

options.text: Treat her faith as a fact of the case: meet with Eleanor and Pastor Obeng together, and consult your attorney on balancing faith and health.
options.outcome: Pastor Obeng, it turns out, takes blood pressure medication himself. 'Sister Eleanor,' he says, holding her hand, 'the Lord works through the pharmacist too.' She resumes the diuretics on Thursday.
options.explanation: The Handbook is direct on this: if a conservatee's religion relies on prayer for healing, those beliefs must be respected, and the conservator should consult a lawyer about balancing religious preferences with health care duties. Religion is part of who Eleanor is — person-centered practice means engaging her belief system and its trusted figures rather than overriding them. Often the perceived conflict between faith and treatment dissolves when explored respectfully from inside the tradition.

options.text: Respect her refusal completely and instruct the facility to discontinue the diuretics, carefully documenting that the conservatee herself declined the treatment.
options.outcome: Her refusal is honored — but within two weeks she's back in the ER with fluid overload, and you realize no one ever explored whether a middle path existed.
options.explanation: This is defensible on its face: without exclusive medical authority, a conservatee retains the right to refuse treatment, and respecting refusal is the legally cautious reflex. But it is inferior because it treats the refusal as the end of the conversation instead of the beginning. The fiduciary's duty of medical advocacy requires exploring the refusal — its sincerity, her understanding, faith-compatible alternatives, clergy involvement — before accepting a foreseeable harm. Respect means engagement, not abandonment.

options.text: Direct the facility to administer the diuretics over her objection — her heart condition is far too serious to leave hostage to a religious idea.
options.outcome: The facility refuses your instruction, correctly noting that no one has authority to force medication on her. Samuel files a complaint describing you as hostile to his mother's faith.
options.explanation: Without a court grant of exclusive medical authority, the conservator cannot force treatment on a refusing conservatee — and dismissing a lifelong faith as 'religious ideas' violates the duty to respect the person's values and religious expression, which is among the rights retained by every person under conservatorship. This response is wrong on the law and wrong on the ethics simultaneously.

stages.narrative: Months later, Eleanor is hospitalized with pneumonia. A POLST in her chart, signed during a prior admission, marks DNR. The overnight resident tells you antibiotics seem 'inconsistent with her code status' and suggests comfort-only measures. Eleanor is febrile but squeezes your hand when you say her name.
stages.prompt: The resident is treating the DNR as a reason to withhold antibiotics. What do you do?

options.text: Advocate at once: DNR means no CPR, not no antibiotics, and ask the attending to confirm a plan treating the pneumonia.
options.outcome: The attending agrees without hesitation, orders antibiotics, and thanks you for catching it. Eleanor is sitting up and complaining about the food within four days.
options.explanation: This is the classic exam distinction: DNR means 'Do Not Resuscitate' — a limit on CPR only — and does NOT mean 'do not treat.' Pneumonia in a DNR patient is still treated unless the patient's directive says otherwise, and Eleanor's living will requests treatment short of resuscitation and artificial life support. Medical advocacy is a core conservator duty: ensuring the person receives proper care sometimes means respectfully correcting the care team.

options.text: Request an ethics committee consultation to formally resolve the disagreement about what her code status permits before any antibiotics are started.
options.outcome: The committee convenes in two days and reaches the obvious conclusion — DNR does not bar antibiotics — but Eleanor spent those two days undertreated.
options.explanation: Ethics consults are a legitimate, sometimes essential tool for genuinely contested questions. But this question isn't genuinely contested — the DNR/do-not-treat distinction is settled, and the directive is clear. Escalating to a committee what a firm advocacy conversation with the attending would resolve today delays needed treatment. The conservator's advocacy duty is exercised at the bedside first; committees are for true dilemmas.

options.text: Defer to the resident's reading of the chart — hospital physicians understand code status better than you do — and consent to the comfort-only measures he proposes.
options.outcome: Eleanor deteriorates from an infection that antibiotics likely would have cleared. Ruth, the ICU nurse, reads the chart and demands to know why nobody pushed back.
options.explanation: Deference to clinicians is appropriate on clinical questions, but what the DNR permits is not purely clinical — it is exactly the legal-ethical boundary the conservator is appointed to guard. A surrogate who rubber-stamps a misreading of the directive fails the medical advocacy duty and converts a no-CPR order into a no-care order the person never chose.

stages.narrative: Winter comes hard. A major stroke leaves Eleanor unresponsive, and this time the fog does not lift. The team raises artificial nutrition — a feeding tube. Her living will declines artificial nutrition and hydration in the event of irreversible incapacity. Samuel pleads: 'A feeding tube isn't giving up. Mama would never choose to starve.' Ruth, exhausted, says, 'Read the document, Sam. She already chose.'
stages.prompt: On what basis do you make the feeding tube decision?

options.text: Apply substituted judgment: her living will declines artificial nutrition in exactly this circumstance, so you decline the tube.
options.outcome: The tube is declined; chaplaincy and hospice come alongside. Samuel grieves the decision but admits the handwriting on the directive is unmistakably his mother's.
options.explanation: Substituted judgment — what the person would decide if able, based on reliable evidence of her wishes — comes BEFORE the best interest standard, which is reserved for when the person's wishes are unknown. Here her wishes are not unknown: a valid directive squarely addresses artificial nutrition, reinforced by her consistent statements. The conservator's duty is to honor the directive, not to relitigate it through a grieving family's preferences — or his own.

options.text: Weigh the team's prognosis, the family's positions, and her quality of life, and make the call under the best interest standard as a neutral, objective tiebreaker.
options.outcome: Your best-interest analysis happens to reach the same outcome as her directive — this time. But Eleanor's counsel notes your reasoning bypassed the document entirely, and asks what you'd have done if 'objective' had pointed the other way.
options.explanation: Best interest is a real, legitimate standard — objective, reasonable-person based — and weighing prognosis and quality of life is exactly how it works. The error is sequencing: best interest applies only when substituted judgment is unavailable. With a directive on point, reaching for best interest substitutes a reasonable person for the actual person. The exam tests this ordering relentlessly: known wishes first, objective standards only in their absence.

options.text: Authorize the feeding tube — Samuel is by far the more insistent voice in the room, and keeping the family at peace serves everyone, including Eleanor.
options.outcome: Eleanor receives the intervention she expressly declined in writing. Ruth retains counsel, and the court is asked to review every surrogate decision you've made.
options.explanation: Surrogate decisions belong to the conservatee's wishes and interests, not to the loudest grief in the room. Honoring advance directives is the duty; family peace is a hoped-for byproduct, never the standard. Overriding a clear directive to appease a relative is a textbook failure of both substituted judgment and fiduciary loyalty.

stages.narrative: Eleanor's pneumonia returns and she is placed on a ventilator during an ER crisis before anyone can be reached. Days pass without improvement. Her living will declined artificial nutrition — but it is silent on mechanical ventilation, and it named no surviving agent. The hospital asks you, as conservator, to authorize withdrawal. Samuel and Ruth, for the first time, agree: 'She's already gone. Let her rest.' You have no exclusive medical authority.
stages.prompt: The ventilator decision is yours to handle. How do you proceed?

options.text: Petition the court for expedited instructions — the directive is silent on ventilation and life support without specific instructions needs court authority.
options.outcome: The court hears the matter within days, finds the withdrawal consistent with Eleanor's documented values, and authorizes it. She dies peacefully, hymns playing, both children at her side — with no legal cloud over the decision.
options.explanation: Use or withdrawal of life support without specific instructions from the conservatee is an extraordinary medical decision requiring court authority — it sits alongside sterilization and experimental treatment on the list of decisions a conservator may not make unilaterally. The directive's silence on ventilation is precisely the gap that triggers the requirement. Seeking instructions is not bureaucratic delay; it is how the law ensures the gravest decision is made with full process, and it protects Eleanor, the family, and the fiduciary alike.

options.text: Rely on the unanimous family, the physicians' consensus, and the clear spirit of her directive, and authorize the withdrawal yourself — any court would obviously reach the same result.
options.outcome: The withdrawal proceeds and no one objects — but at your final report, the court notes you exercised an authority you did not hold, and that the absence of harm was good fortune, not good practice.
options.explanation: Everything substantive here is right: the consensus is genuine, the values evidence strong, and a court likely would approve. That is exactly what makes this option seductive — and still wrong. The conservator simply lacks unilateral authority over life support absent the conservatee's specific instructions or a court order, and unanimity does not confer it. When the law assigns the final word to the court, the better fiduciary brings the strong record to the judge rather than acting on the prediction.

options.text: Refuse to engage with the question and direct that full treatment continue indefinitely — withdrawal of life support is simply too dangerous for a conservator to touch.
options.outcome: Weeks pass. Eleanor remains suspended on a machine in a state she would never have chosen, while the family's grief curdles into anger at the system — and at you.
options.explanation: Declining to decide is itself a decision — for continued intervention the evidence says she would refuse. The conservator cannot unilaterally withdraw life support, but he absolutely can and should bring the question to the court. Paralysis abandons the advocacy duty and the substituted-judgment evidence, prolonging exactly the kind of mechanized dying her directive sought to avoid.

epilogues.triumph: At the discharge hearing, the judge says something rarely heard in probate court: 'This is what the statute hopes for.' Eleanor died as she chose — faith honored, directive followed, family intact enough to sit on the same bench. Pastor Obeng asks if he can refer his congregation's elders to you. Ruth already has.
epilogues.solid: Eleanor's passing was peaceful, and the major decisions landed where her directive pointed, even if the path wandered. The court approves your final report with a gentle reminder about sequencing — wishes first, standards second, court when the law requires it.
epilogues.shaky: The outcome was survivable but the record is uncomfortable: decisions made before documents were found, advocacy that arrived late, authority stretched past its edges. The court approves the final account while noting 'significant concerns' about your handling of end-of-life process, and Eleanor's counsel files a copy with the Bureau.
epilogues.disaster: Between the overridden directive and the off-record withdrawal attempt, the court removes you before Eleanor's final months are out. Her last season becomes a legal battlefield — the precise outcome a conservator of the person exists to prevent — and the Bureau's accusation arrives by certified mail.

title: The House on Magnolia Street
tagline: Two children, two plans, one mother who just wants to stay home. The law has an opinion — do you know it?

client.name: Lien Tran
client.snapshot: Mrs. Tran came to San Jose from Vietnam in 1981 and raised two children in the little house on Magnolia Street, where the kitchen always smells of lemongrass and the Buddhist altar holds her late husband's photograph. A fall and a hip fracture revealed moderate dementia. Her daughter Kim wants her in a nursing facility near Kim's home in Walnut Creek; her son Daniel insists she stay on Magnolia Street, whatever it takes.

intro: You are appointed conservator of Mrs. Tran's person and estate after Kim and Daniel's competing petitions convinced the judge that neither should serve. Your first visit is to the rehab unit, where Mrs. Tran is recovering from hip surgery. Through the Vietnamese interpreter, she tells you three things: she wants to go home, she wants her morning tea on the back porch, and she wants to know who is feeding the koi. The discharge planner catches you in the hallway with a different message: 'She's a fall risk. We're recommending skilled nursing. We need your decision by Friday.'

stages.narrative: Friday is three days away. Kim emails you a brochure for a five-star SNF in Walnut Creek with an open bed. Daniel texts that he'll 'fight any placement in court.' The discharge planner calls again before lunch.
stages.prompt: What do you do before making any decision about where Mrs. Tran goes after rehab?

options.text: Commission a real functional assessment first — ADLs and IADLs, a cognition workup, a home safety visit, and her own input through the interpreter.
options.outcome: The picture sharpens: she needs help bathing and with medications, walks safely with a walker on flat ground, and lights up when describing her porch routine. The house needs grab bars and a ramp — not abandonment.
options.explanation: A functional assessment is the diagnostic foundation of every placement decision — a multidimensional picture of how the person actually functions, drawn from your own observation, professional evaluations, facility input, and the person herself. Conservatorship decisions rest on decisional capacity and demonstrated function, not diagnosis or a single professional's recommendation. Services appropriate for one person may be wrong for another; you cannot know which without assessing this person, in her real context, including her home.

options.text: Adopt the rehab team's discharge recommendation — they've observed her daily for three weeks, and their clinical judgment is that she needs skilled nursing care.
options.outcome: You accept the SNF recommendation. Only later do you learn discharge planners never saw her house, never used an interpreter for more than logistics, and scored her 'confused' partly because she answers in Vietnamese when tired.
options.explanation: Relying on the team with the most clinical contact is reasonable and defensible — their input is a necessary part of the assessment. But it is inferior because it is one source where the law expects a multidimensional picture: the rehab unit sees a hospital patient, not the woman in her own kitchen with familiar supports. Institutional assessments systematically miss home context, language, and culture; the conservator's job is to assemble the whole picture, not subcontract it.

options.text: Go with Kim's plan — she's the daughter who visits most, and the Walnut Creek facility has an open bed that won't stay open if you wait around.
options.outcome: Daniel's attorney is in front of the judge within two weeks, asking why the conservator made a placement decision based on one child's preference and a brochure.
options.explanation: Family input matters, but a placement decision driven by one relative's convenience and bed availability gets the analysis backwards. The decision must rest on Mrs. Tran's assessed needs and preferences — the very reason a neutral professional was appointed over the warring siblings was to break the pattern of decisions made about her without her.

stages.narrative: The assessment is done. With grab bars, a ramp, medication management, and daily caregiver hours, the team agrees Mrs. Tran could return to Magnolia Street safely — at a cost the estate can sustain for now. Kim is furious: 'One fall and this is all on you.' Daniel is triumphant. Mrs. Tran asks again about the koi.
stages.prompt: What placement do you choose, and on what legal footing?
stages.subtopic: Least Restrictive Alternative & the Personal Residence Preference

options.text: Return her home with the support package — the law prefers the personal residence and the least restrictive setting, and the assessment shows home works.
options.outcome: Mrs. Tran comes home to her porch, her altar, and her koi. The caregiver learns how she takes her tea. Kim remains skeptical but admits her mother sounds like herself again on the phone.
options.explanation: California law presumes the conservatee's personal residence — the home she regarded as permanent at the time of the petition — is the least restrictive appropriate residence, and the conservator must determine whether she can stay there with supports. The least restrictive alternative principle requires the setting that limits her rights and freedoms least while meeting her needs, decided by her needs and preferences, not the family's comfort. With an assessment showing feasibility, home is not just sentiment — it is the legal default.

options.text: Choose a well-regarded RCFE in San Jose — a middle path less restrictive than the SNF Kim wants, keeping her in her community while removing the fall risks of the aging house.
options.outcome: The RCFE is genuinely pleasant. But Mrs. Tran asks the staff weekly when she's going home, and you find yourself unable to explain — to her or to the court — why home with supports wasn't tried first.
options.explanation: An assisted-living compromise is attractive: safer than the house, freer than a SNF, and it would satisfy most observers. But it is inferior because the law's preference isn't 'a reasonably unrestrictive setting' — it is her personal residence specifically, when it can appropriately meet her needs. Your own assessment said it could. Skipping the legally preferred option for a defensible-sounding compromise is exactly the better-versus-best distinction the exam tests: the move to any facility requires justification grounded in her needs, and 'the house is old' isn't it.

options.text: Return her home but skip the support package to preserve the estate — Daniel says he'll 'check on her most days,' which keeps her on Magnolia Street at no cost.
options.outcome: Daniel's 'most days' becomes most weeks. Mrs. Tran misses medications, the second fall happens in the bathroom, and this time the hospital social worker files a report questioning the conservator's arrangements.
options.explanation: Returning a person with assessed care needs to an unsupported environment is neglect with a smile on it. The least restrictive alternative means the least restrictive setting that meets her needs — stripping out the services that made home appropriate makes the placement inappropriate. A conservator who substitutes a relative's vague promises for an assessed care plan has failed the most basic well-being oversight duty.

stages.narrative: Settled at home, Mrs. Tran tells you through the interpreter that she wants to change her will: the Magnolia Street house should go to her grandson Minh, 'who loves the garden.' Kim, hearing of it, calls you immediately: 'She's conserved. She can't legally do that — and you shouldn't let her.'
stages.prompt: How do you respond to Mrs. Tran's wish to change her will?

options.text: Tell Kim she's wrong — conservatees keep the right to make a will — and arrange an independent attorney to assess capacity while you stay out of the contents.
options.outcome: The attorney meets with Mrs. Tran alone with an interpreter, finds she understands her property and her family, and prepares the codicil. You note the referral in your records — and nothing more.
options.explanation: Appointment of a conservator does not strip testamentary rights: the conservatee retains the right to make or amend a will, and the right to marry, unless a judge specifically finds otherwise. Testamentary capacity is a distinct, relatively low threshold — knowing one's property and natural heirs — that a person with moderate dementia may well retain, and it is the independent attorney's call, not the conservator's or the family's. The fiduciary's role is to facilitate the retained right and keep his hands entirely off the dispositive choices.

options.text: Before involving any attorney, petition the court for instructions on whether Mrs. Tran may execute a codicil, so that no one can later question the process you followed.
options.outcome: The court's response arrives months later and amounts to a shrug: the right is retained, the capacity question belongs to the drafting attorney, and the petition was unnecessary — at the estate's expense.
options.explanation: Seeking court guidance when uncertain is generally sound fiduciary instinct, and it's far better than blocking her. But it is inferior here because the law is not uncertain: the right to make or amend a will is expressly retained by conservatees. Petitioning the court to permit what the law already permits delays her exercise of a retained right and spends her money on a question with a known answer. Good judgment includes knowing when the rulebook is already clear.

options.text: Tell Mrs. Tran gently that the conservatorship means decisions like this are handled for her now, and that she can revisit it if her rights are ever restored.
options.outcome: Mrs. Tran stops raising the subject — and stops raising other things too, having absorbed the lesson that her wishes are no longer operative. The codicil never happens; Minh never knows.
options.explanation: This misstates the law and inflicts the exact harm conservatorship reform exists to prevent: treating appointment as the erasure of all civil rights. Conservatees retain enumerated rights — wills, marriage, mail, counsel, control of wages — and the conservator is supposed to be their guardian, not their gatekeeper. Wrongly telling a person she has lost a right she retains is a quiet but profound rights violation.

stages.narrative: Two years pass well. Then the dementia advances: Mrs. Tran begins wandering at night, the caregiver finds the stove on at 3 a.m., and the care team agrees the house — even with supports — no longer meets her needs. An RCFE with a memory care wing four miles away, run by a Vietnamese-American family, has an opening in five weeks. Kim and Daniel, for once, both agree it's time.
stages.prompt: The move from her personal residence is now genuinely necessary. How do you carry it out?

options.text: Give the required prior notice to the court and those close to her, document the reasons, and use the five weeks for a person-centered transition.
options.outcome: No one objects to the noticed move. Mrs. Tran arrives at a room that already smells like home, with her husband's photograph on the dresser, and asks if the koi can visit.
options.explanation: A move from the conservatee's personal residence requires prior notice to the court and to those close to her, and the reasons must be grounded in her needs and preferences — never the convenience of others. The five-week runway makes full compliance easy, and the same window serves the second duty: relocation stress is a recognized, sometimes dangerous phenomenon in cognitively impaired elders, and a planned transition with familiar objects, advance visits, and overlapping caregivers is how person-centered practice mitigates it. Legal compliance and humane transition are the same project here.

options.text: File the notice properly, then execute the move the day the bed opens — efficient and fully compliant, leaving the adjustment itself to the facility's experienced memory care staff.
options.outcome: The paperwork is flawless. But Mrs. Tran arrives at a bare room among strangers, and the first month is marked by the weight loss and withdrawal a planned transition might have softened.
options.explanation: This satisfies the legal requirement — prior notice given, needs-based reasons documented — and trusting professional memory care staff is not unreasonable. It is inferior because compliance is the floor, not the standard: relocation stress is foreseeable and partially preventable, and person-centered planning obligates the conservator to manage the human transition, not just the legal one. The difference between this and the best answer is the difference between moving a case and moving a person.

options.text: Move her the week the bed opens and file the notice afterward — good memory care beds are scarce, and the court will understand a fait accompli backed by sound reasons.
options.outcome: The court does not understand. The judge notes that five weeks was ample time for prior notice, asks what else gets done in the wrong order in your practice, and orders enhanced reporting.
options.explanation: The notice requirement is prior notice — it exists so the court and people who care about her can weigh in before the most consequential personal decision in a conservatorship, not ratify it after. Only a genuine emergency justifies move-first procedures, and a scheduled vacancy five weeks out is the opposite of an emergency. Treating safeguards as paperwork to backfill is how conservators earn the court's lasting suspicion.

stages.narrative: Before you finalize the contract, Kim makes one last push: 'Memory care today, but what about next year? Just put her in a skilled nursing facility now so we never have to move her again. One move, done.' The geriatrician's latest evaluation, meanwhile, shows she needs supervision and personal care assistance — not nursing care.
stages.prompt: Kim wants to skip assisted living and go straight to a SNF. How do you decide the level of care?
stages.subtopic: RCFE vs. SNF Levels of Care

options.text: Match placement to her needs today — the RCFE memory care unit, the least restrictive fit — and commit to reevaluating the level of care as she changes.
options.outcome: Mrs. Tran settles into the RCFE, where she can still walk the garden with supervision and help fold towels in the afternoon — abilities a nursing bed would have idled. The reevaluation plan goes in your care file.
options.explanation: An RCFE (assisted living, licensed by the Department of Social Services) serves people needing supervision and personal care; a SNF provides nursing-level medical care. Her assessment calls for the former. The least restrictive alternative analysis is continuous, not one-time: the conservator must reevaluate when significant changes occur and adjust the placement then. Pre-positioning her in an over-restrictive setting to economize on future moves trades her present freedom for the family's future convenience — precisely the trade the standard forbids.

options.text: Choose a larger continuing-care campus offering assisted living through skilled nursing, even with a weaker memory program across town, so she can age in place without future moves.
options.outcome: The campus model works administratively. But the staff turnover is high, no one speaks Vietnamese, and the lemongrass-and-incense familiarity of the family-run RCFE — the thing that made her last placement feel like a home — has no equivalent here.
options.explanation: The continuum-of-care logic is genuinely sound — minimizing future relocations is a legitimate consideration for a progressive disease, and this is a defensible professional choice. It is inferior because it subordinates the person-centered factors that the assessment elevated: cultural and linguistic fit, community proximity, and program quality for her actual present needs. Placement decisions weigh facility factors — licensing, staffing, activities, fit — for this person; a structurally elegant option that serves her worse today is the lesser choice.

options.text: Take Kim's deal and admit her to the Walnut Creek SNF now — she'll probably need that level eventually, and the family harmony it buys has its own real value.
options.outcome: In a nursing unit built for bed-bound patients, Mrs. Tran's remaining independence has nowhere to go. Six months in, she no longer dresses herself — not because she can't, but because no one waits long enough to let her.
options.explanation: Placing a person at a higher level of care than assessed needs require violates the least restrictive alternative standard and accelerates the very decline it anticipates — excess care de-skills. The justification is the family's convenience and conflict-avoidance, not her needs, failing the required basis for residential decisions. 'She'll need it eventually' is an argument for monitoring and reevaluation, never for premature restriction.

stages.narrative: Three weeks after the move, the RCFE reports Mrs. Tran has lost four pounds and rarely leaves her room. The same week, Daniel — who opposed every facility from the start — shows up after visiting hours smelling of beer, argues with staff, and tells his mother in Vietnamese that her children are trying to erase her. Kim demands you ban him from the facility.
stages.prompt: You have a declining resident and an escalating family conflict. What do you do?

options.text: Work both: treat the weight loss as relocation stress needing active response, and address Daniel directly with visiting expectations rather than a ban.
options.outcome: The temple ladies start coming Tuesdays; the kitchen learns her congee. Daniel, given an actual role — he takes over the garden visits — stops arriving angry. The weight comes back by month's end.
options.explanation: Relocation stress in a cognitively impaired elder is a recognized clinical risk that demands active intervention, not waiting — continuity of culture, language, faith, and relationships is the treatment. On the family side, access disputes deserve immediate attention but the conservatee's rights frame the response: she has the right to receive visitors, and Daniel's visits — however irritating to staff — are her connection to her son. The conservator manages the behavior and preserves the relationship, restricting access only if she is actually being harmed and then with court involvement.

options.text: Focus on the clinical decline first — physician evaluation, dietary consult, activity plan — and let the facility's own visitor policies deal with Daniel for the time being.
options.outcome: Her weight stabilizes under the clinical plan. But the facility, left alone with Daniel, bars him after the next incident — and Mrs. Tran, asking for her son nightly, can't understand where he went.
options.explanation: Prioritizing the medical response is sound, and the clinical plan is exactly right. It is inferior because it treats the family conflict as someone else's problem when access disputes are squarely the conservator's to manage — they deserve immediate attention and they directly affect her well-being, as her nightly asking shows. Delegating Daniel to facility policy predictably produces a ban that punishes her, when the conservator was positioned to broker something better.

options.text: Give Kim what she's asking for and instruct the facility to remove Daniel from the visitor list until he can demonstrate stability to everyone's satisfaction.
options.outcome: Daniel's attorney cites the conservatee's right to receive visitors, and the court asks what evidence showed his visits harmed her — as opposed to annoying his sister and the staff.
options.explanation: Conservatees retain the right to receive visitors, phone calls, and mail unless the court specifically limits them; a conservator cannot informally cut off a child's access at the other child's demand. The standard is harm to her, not friction with staff or family politics — and unilaterally severing her closest relationship is more likely to deepen her decline than relieve it. Restrictions of this kind, where genuinely needed, run through the court.

epilogues.triumph: At the biennial review, the court investigator's report on Mrs. Tran reads less like a case file than a life: home as long as home could hold her, a lawful move handled with grace, rights intact, both children — somehow — still speaking. The judge asks if you'd consider taking court referrals for contested family cases. Kim and Daniel split the cost of a gift basket, which may be the greater miracle.
epilogues.solid: Mrs. Tran is safe, settled, and as content as her condition allows, though a few decisions took the long way around. The court approves your reports, the family truce holds most weeks, and the koi — under Minh's care now — are thriving.
epilogues.shaky: The placements ultimately landed in defensible places, but the route ran through skipped preferences, late notices, and a family conflict left to burn. The court orders more frequent status reports and pointedly reminds you that the personal residence preference 'is not advisory.' Daniel's attorney keeps the file open.
epilogues.disaster: An over-restrictive placement, a backdated notice, and a documented decline nobody acted on: the court removes you as conservator and surcharges the estate's avoidable rehab and facility costs against your fees. Mrs. Tran's third conservator in four years starts by asking what happened to the house on Magnolia Street.

title: The Caregiver's Shadow
tagline: Frank's caregiver came with the highest recommendations. The bruise on his wrist tells a different story.

client.name: Frank Kowalski
client.snapshot: Frank is a retired machinist and widower with Parkinson's disease and mild cognitive impairment, living in the Sacramento bungalow he bought in 1974. Fiercely independent and stubborn about it, he relies on Vera, a live-in caregiver hired by his late wife three years ago. His only relative is a niece in Oregon who calls on Sundays.

intro: You are appointed conservator of Frank's person and estate after his bank flagged unusual account activity and a neighbor's call to the court raised concerns no one followed up on for months. Your Letters were issued Tuesday. Wednesday, you stand on Frank's porch for the first time. Vera answers the door before you knock, smiling, and explains that Frank is 'having one of his foggy days' and that she handles 'everything — bills, meds, all of it, so he doesn't worry.' Behind her, in the dim living room, Frank lifts a trembling hand in something between a wave and a question.

stages.narrative: Vera follows you into every room. The house is clean enough, the refrigerator stocked. Frank answers questions by glancing at Vera first. Your appointment is days old, and the court's clock is already running.
stages.prompt: What do you do in the first weeks to establish Frank's actual situation?

options.text: Run your own needs assessment — time alone with Frank, a functional evaluation, a meds and finance review — and start the care plan the court requires within 120 days.
options.outcome: Alone on the back steps, Frank is sharper than advertised — and quieter about Vera than a contented man would be. Your assessment is complete by week six — ample runway before the 120-day care plan deadline — documenting that home remains appropriate with changes you're now investigating.
options.explanation: Under SB 280 (effective 2025), the appropriate level of care is determined upon appointment, and the conservator must file a written care plan within 120 calendar days of appointment (Prob. Code §§2351.2, 2352.5) — evaluating his care level and what's necessary to keep him in his personal residence. The assessment itself must be yours, not the caregiver's narration: information from your own observation, professional evaluations, and the person himself, interviewed where he can speak freely. A conservatee who checks with the caregiver before answering is itself a finding.

options.text: Since the household looks stable, leave the current arrangements in place, observe for a few months, and complete the formal assessment as part of your first annual review.
options.outcome: The household stays calm — and the 120-day care plan deadline passes unmarked. The court's deficiency notice arrives before your 'few months' do, and the observation period gave Vera time you didn't know you were giving her.
options.explanation: Not disrupting a seemingly functional arrangement is a reasonable instinct — stability has real value for a man with Parkinson's. But it is inferior because the care plan is a 120-day statutory filing, not an annual-review item, and because 'appears stable' was Vera's presentation, not your assessment. The early weeks are precisely when an independent baseline matters most: every month of deferred assessment is a month of unverified assumptions.

options.text: Save the estate the evaluation costs — Vera has run everything for three years — and take her detailed verbal report on Frank's condition as your assessment baseline.
options.outcome: Your file now contains, as its foundational document, the unverified account of the person every later question will be about.
options.explanation: An assessment sourced entirely from the caregiver is not an assessment — it is dictation. The conservator's monitoring role exists because the people closest to a dependent adult are both the likeliest helpers and the likeliest exploiters; independent verification is the entire point. Building the case file on Vera's narrative compromises every subsequent judgment and would embarrass you in front of any court investigator.

stages.narrative: The assessment lands: Frank needs medication management, fall prevention, help bathing, and more social contact than a TV and one caregiver provide. He tells you, alone, that he wants to die in this house 'like Helen did,' that he misses his machinist club, and that Vera 'does fine, mostly.' It's time to put structure around his care.
stages.prompt: How do you build Frank's care plan?

options.text: Draft the written plan with Frank at the table — health, meals, personal care, the club — matched to a financial plan and reviewed at least annually.
options.outcome: Frank, asked his opinion for the first time in years, has plenty of them. The plan that emerges has Tuesday club meetings in it, and he signs the copy you leave him with exaggerated ceremony.
options.explanation: A care plan should cover the full span — living situation, health care, meals, clothing, personal care, recreation, social activities — paired with a financial plan identifying how it's funded short- and long-term, and reviewed at least annually or when significant changes occur. Person-centered planning means Frank's preferences are the focal point and he participates to the greatest extent possible: the plan exists to support his life, including the parts (the club, dying at home like Helen) that no checklist would have surfaced without asking him.

options.text: Build a clinically thorough plan from the professional assessments — medication protocols, fall modifications, bathing help, scheduled socialization — and present the finished plan to Frank for his information.
options.outcome: The plan is professionally impeccable. Frank complies with it the way men like Frank comply with things done to them — minimally, and with the club meetings he'd have told you about left undiscovered for months.
options.explanation: A clinically rigorous plan covering all the right domains is real fiduciary work, and most courts would accept it. It is inferior because it inverts person-centered planning: the person is the source of the plan, not its audience. The NGA principles require involving the person in decisions to the greatest extent possible — and practically, plans built with the person get followed, while plans presented to him get endured. The missing ingredient isn't competence; it's the conversation.

options.text: Keep the planning informal — you already know what he needs, the needs live in your head, and extra paperwork shouldn't bill hours against his estate.
options.outcome: Eight months later you can't reconstruct what was decided about medication supervision or when, and the court investigator's question — 'May I see the care plan?' — has no good answer.
options.explanation: The court now mandates exactly this paperwork — SB 280 requires the care plan to be filed within 120 days of appointment (Prob. Code §2352.5) — and beyond compliance, an undocumented plan can't be communicated to providers, reviewed against changes, or defended to the court. The fiduciary standard requires an open book with paper trails. 'It's in my head' fails the moment anyone — a doctor, a successor, a judge — needs to know what the plan is, which is the only time it matters.

stages.narrative: You make your visits weekly and unannounced. On the fourth one, the pattern surfaces: a bruise ringing Frank's wrist he says came from 'grabbing wrong,' a medication log with gaps every weekend, and — at the bank — three checks to 'cash' in Vera's handwriting with Frank's wavering signature, plus a new ATM card he doesn't remember requesting. When you mention the checks, Frank looks at the door and asks you to keep your voice down.
stages.prompt: Your monitoring has surfaced multiple red flags. What does this stage of oversight require?

options.text: Treat the cluster as a signal: document with photos, have the physician examine the bruising, secure the accounts, and interview Frank where Vera can't hear.
options.outcome: The physician documents grip-pattern bruising 'inconsistent with a fall.' Frank, in the doctor's office with the door closed, finally says it: Vera's boyfriend has been staying weekends, and the weekends are when things go wrong.
options.explanation: Unexplained bruises, fearfulness toward a caregiver, medication irregularities, checks to cash, and unfamiliar account instruments are textbook signs of abuse and financial exploitation — and a cluster of them is a presumption to investigate, not a coincidence to explain away. The oversight playbook is concrete: document, involve the physician, speak with the person safely and privately, and secure the finances. Sequencing matters too — protective steps before confrontation, so the vulnerable person isn't left alone with an alerted abuser.

options.text: Raise each item with Vera directly and give her a chance to explain — the bruise, the weekend gaps, the checks — while you tighten the financial controls and increase your visit frequency.
options.outcome: Vera has answers for everything, delivered smoothly. She also now knows exactly what you've noticed — and that weekend, the medication log is suddenly perfect, the boyfriend invisible, and Frank more careful than ever about his words.
options.explanation: Seeking the caregiver's explanation seems like basic fairness, and tightening controls and monitoring are genuinely right. It is inferior because confronting a suspected abuser before the vulnerable person is protected hands the suspect the investigation: evidence gets sanitized, the conservatee gets coached or silenced, and the window for candid disclosure closes. Fairness to Vera comes later, through process; protection of Frank comes first, through sequence.

options.text: Note your concerns in the file and keep watching — bruises happen to men with Parkinson's, and accusing a three-year caregiver on circumstantial signs could blow up his support system.
options.outcome: Two more 'grabbing wrong' bruises accumulate in your file, beautifully documented, while the thing causing them continues uninterrupted.
options.explanation: Each sign alone might be innocent; the cluster is not dismissible, and 'keep watching' is what the system did before you were appointed — it's why you were appointed. Monitoring without acting converts the conservator from protector to chronicler. The threshold for investigating is reasonable concern, not certainty; waiting for proof means waiting for harm.

stages.narrative: The physician's findings and the bank records sit on your desk. It's no longer a hunch; it's reasonable suspicion of physical abuse and financial exploitation of an elder. Frank, ashamed, begs you: 'Don't make it official. She'll be angry. And I don't want strangers in my business.' You're his fiduciary — and his confidant — and he has just asked you for silence.
stages.prompt: Frank has asked you to keep the abuse confidential. What do you do?

options.text: Tell Frank what you must do and why — you're a mandated reporter and abuse is the exception to confidentiality — then file the APS and police reports and secure his safety the same day.
options.outcome: Frank is angry for a week — then, when the APS investigator turns out to be patient and Vera's boyfriend turns out to have a record, quietly relieved someone else made the call he couldn't. The safety plan holds.
options.explanation: The confidentiality duty has exactly this exception: a fiduciary must disclose abuse, neglect, or exploitation, and as a conservator you are a mandated reporter — reporting is a legal obligation, not a judgment call, and there is no conflict of interest in a fiduciary filing an APS report. Honoring the person includes honesty about the limits of confidence and pairing the report with real protective action. A report that leaves the abuser in the house is paperwork; the same-day safety plan is what makes it protection.

options.text: File the APS report as required, but spare Frank the confrontation: submit it without telling him, let the investigation arrive as if routine, and keep your relationship with him uncomplicated.
options.outcome: The report is filed on time and the system works. But when the investigator knocks, Frank realizes you went around him — and the confidant who handled his shame by managing him quietly joins the list of people who decide things about Frank without Frank.
options.explanation: The legal duty is fully satisfied — the report is filed, protection initiated, and shielding a distressed client from anticipated conflict is a humane instinct. It is inferior because it spends the relationship to buy the comfort: dignity and respect mean telling the person what you must do with what he told you, even when the conversation is hard. Frank's trust is a clinical asset for everything that follows — placements, care decisions, the next disclosure — and deception-by-omission is a costly way to avoid one painful talk.

options.text: Honor his autonomy — he's the client and the wish is clearly his — and handle it privately: dismiss Vera with severance, change the locks, and write 'resolved internally' in the file.
options.outcome: Vera moves on — directly into a live-in position with another elderly client across town, trailing the spotless reference of never having been reported.
options.explanation: Client direction cannot waive a mandated report: the reporting duty is the fiduciary's own legal obligation, triggered by reasonable suspicion, and it exists precisely because abused elders are often pressured or ashamed into requesting silence. 'Respecting his wishes' here abandons both the law and the broader protective system — APS exists partly so the Veras of the world don't simply relocate. Autonomy governs many fiduciary decisions; this is one of the few it cannot.

stages.narrative: Vera is gone, APS substantiates the financial abuse, and the DA's office takes the theft file. Now the practical problem: Frank is alone in the bungalow he refuses to leave, needing daily help, on a fixed income with a depleted estate — he receives Social Security and, as it turns out, qualifies for Medi-Cal. His niece suggests 'one of those nice facilities.' Frank suggests, colorfully, otherwise.
stages.prompt: How do you rebuild Frank's care at home with the estate's reduced means?

options.text: Layer the resources he's entitled to — apply for IHSS, then add Meals on Wheels, paratransit to the club, a day program, and a vetted aide for the gaps.
options.outcome: The county authorizes substantial weekly IHSS hours; the day program gives Tuesdays a shape again. Frank stays in the bungalow, the budget balances, and the niece concedes that 'those facility brochures can wait.'
options.explanation: IHSS is built for exactly this: it pays for in-home services — personal care, meal preparation, housecleaning, accompaniment to medical visits, protective supervision — for Medi-Cal recipients living in a home of their own choosing, with a county social worker assessing needs and authorizing hours (up to a monthly maximum of 283 hours for severely impaired recipients, 195 otherwise). Knowledge of community resources — meals, transportation, day programs, respite — is a core conservator competency precisely because it is what makes the least restrictive option affordable. The cheapest plan and the most person-centered plan are, here, the same plan.

options.text: Move him to a modest RCFE — after a live-in caregiver just exploited him in that house, a licensed facility with staff and oversight is the safer architecture, even over his objection.
options.outcome: The facility is decent and genuinely safe. But Frank — who told you he wants to die in that house like Helen did — goes quiet in a way that has nothing to do with Parkinson's, and you placed him there with an in-home option unexplored on the table.
options.explanation: The risk logic is real: in-home care concentrated in one unsupervised person is exactly what just failed, and a licensed facility's structural oversight is a legitimate protective consideration. It is inferior because it answers the last problem instead of this one — the lesson of Vera is better monitoring and distributed care (agency aides, IHSS workers, day programs, your oversight), not abandoning the legally preferred personal residence that an assessment says can still work. His stated wishes and the least restrictive alternative tip the balance home, with the safeguards built in this time.

options.text: Refer him to the Regional Center — he has a disabling neurological condition, and Regional Centers fund generous in-home supports with no asset test to worry about.
options.outcome: The intake worker explains, kindly, what a study of the Lanterman Act would have: Parkinson's acquired at 80 is not a developmental disability, and Frank is ineligible. Weeks are lost to the wrong door.
options.explanation: Regional Centers serve developmental disabilities — intellectual disability, cerebral palsy, epilepsy, autism, and related conditions originating before age 18 (California’s Lanterman Act cutoff; the federal DD Act uses 22) — and expressly exclude conditions that are solely physical or acquired in later life. Knowing which resource fits which client is the substance of the community-resources competency; a referral that mismatches the eligibility rules costs the client time and the fiduciary credibility, and it signals study of the resource map is overdue.

stages.narrative: Eleven good months follow — the club on Tuesdays, the IHSS aide he grudgingly likes, a restitution order against Vera grinding through the system. Then, on a gray February morning, the aide finds that Frank has died in his sleep, in his own bed, in the house on its quiet street. Like Helen did. The aide calls you first. The niece, in Oregon, asks what happens now.
stages.prompt: Frank has died. What are your duties as conservator now?

options.text: Do the wind-down: file the GC-399 death notice, notify the agencies, secure the property, prepare the final account, and preserve assets for the personal representative.
options.outcome: The GC-399 is filed within days; the house is secured the same morning. The final account balances to the penny, the court grants your discharge, and the niece — now executor — inherits an estate in perfect order and a folder labeled 'Everything you need.'
